According to recent reports, there are some things you know you need before you start training for a marathon, like a good pair of sneakers. But some of the most useful marathon items? You don’t even realize how helpful they are until you’re deep in the thick of training.

According to recent reports, we’re talking the non-glitzy, random products that make life easier when you’re spending multiple days running each week. For me, one of those things is canned salmon. I buy the stuff in bulk because when I get back from a long run, it only takes me 20 seconds to whip the stuff up with some salt, pepper, and mayo and serve it on crackers before I collapse on the couch for a few hours. (It’s a kinda-smelly, but ridiculously simple way to get protein fast.).

According to recent reports, curious what other unexpected finds made a difference, I asked women to share the products they never knew they needed before running a marathon but now can't imagine training without. Check out their answers….

Sources indicate that there is nothing like race day, especially for your first marathon. And, for the most part, you know what you need: Your trusty sneakers, an outfit you’ve hopefully tested during training, your fuel, and your watch. Here are three more things that will help the day go by even better.

“Having your name on a shirt or bib is soooo fun because even strangers will cheer you on along the course! It will help you feel the true energy and vibe of the race.” —Claudette Sariya, 33, Honolulu ’25 (You can use iron-on letters from Amazon, or go through a firm like Pens and Paces to commission your own bib.).

“Rally is a great way to feel supported by your loved ones who can’t make the race, or maybe you don’t have time to stop if you’re going for a personal best. At mile 10 of my first marathon, I was struggling a bit and my mom’s message came through my headphones—I hear her words every time I run a race now. Such a special concept that really enhanced my race day!” — Shannon Kauber, 25, NYC ’25, ’26, Chicago ’26.

“After a race, because I have so many apps running (like Strava, Spotify, and Rally), my battery can be very low, and it sucks when I’m on four percent and looking for friends and family or want to take pictures, so it’s good to have a portable charger just in case. I’m less anxious knowing that I’ll be able to get in touch with people and that my phone is good to go. And if my phone dies randomly, then I’ll have backup juice.” —Sariya (Any charger will work, but Sariya has seen success with Anker brand ones.).

Industry observers note that “I had my boyfriend meet me at the halfway point with a cold towel and it was a game changer. It made me feel instantly more awake and energetic.” —Tianna Soto, 32, NYC ’24, NYC Virtual ’26 (You can stay low-tech and put an old towel in the freezer, or you can opt for a cooling towel that helps you regulate your body temp.).

These products all help remove any uncomfortable rubbing and chafing from their gear to keep you comfortable over many, many miles.

According to recent reports, “I keep it on my bathroom counter so I don’t forget to swipe at minimum inner thighs and inner arms for a training run. Long runs and race days get the full treatment with swipes under any and every seam, around the toes, waistbands, and shoulders under straps. I love traveling with the teeny travel version too.” —Jennifer Nied, 40, NYC ’17, ’19, Chicago ’18, London ’24.

“The bigger ones saved me when I used to get these crazy arch blisters from when I first started running. I usually use those, but I’ve also used the smaller ones for toe blisters.” —Geneve Lau, 27, Marine Corps ’24, NYC ’25, ’26.

Industry observers note that “I swear by [these] soft little tubes that go over your toe to help prevent friction and pressure when you’re running or walking. I just started using them this year, and they’ve saved my pinkie toes during training and the marathon!” —Soto.

It has been revealed that fueling is one of the most vital parts of marathon training, and chances are you've already experimented with your fair share of gels. But sometimes, the foods and snacks you never thought to try end up making the biggest difference.

“I liked clementines as a whole food before moving to gels and chews. Clementine wedges are bite-sized so I wasn’t as worried about choking while running but they weren’t chewy, saving those textures for other fuel. They have water and sugar, though I never did the math on the amount of sugar compared to my needs while training (I know better now). During training, I would toss two whole clementines in my running hydration vest pockets and peel as I ran to occupy my hands/brain with something other than running. On race day, I pre-peeled the food and put the slices in a snack sized ziploc.” —Suzi Berkey Hanson, Chicago ’23.

“As someone with endometriosis and a resulting sensitive G.I. system, taking in a high volume of carbs at any point in time is highly aggravating to my stomach and often causes high levels of nausea, bloating, and discomfort. So, I decided to switch to more solid foods that included a healthy source of fats and proteins mixed in with carbs. In this marathon training block, I would alternate Kind Bars with Honey Stinger Chews which sat much better with my stomach and made my race and post race recovery much more pleasant.” —Winnie Yu, 31, NYC ’23, ’26.

Industry observers note that “I ate one pretty much after every morning run because they were easy to throw in my bag and defrost on the way to work and they’re great for quick carbs. They were also great to eat before a long run because, again, they require basically no prep. When you’re marathon training and working a full-time job sometimes you just gravitate towards whatever is easiest and whatever fits into your routine best but still helps you meet your goals and this was mine” —Andrea Bian, 26, NYC ’25, ’26.

Dogecoin [DOGE] has fallen by over 40% since 22nd September, with the memecoin losing its position among the top-10 cryptos by market cap. In fact, it has fallen by over 12% to a cap of around $9.88 billion over the last seven days, with the price at $0.063 at press time.

In fact, DOGE seemed to be trading in a descending trend channel, with the $0.059-$0.060 level emerging as a key support.

Its daily trading volumes have also fallen significantly. The average net volume was seller-dominated, with 265.5 million DOGE tokens exchanged for USDT on Binance’s spot market.

According to recent reports, similarly, the CMF reading fell from 0.20 to 0.01. Even though the metric was still above the neutral level, the sharp decline hinted at capital flight.

At the time of writing, Dogecoin seemed to be heading towards the slanting trendline support, which runs from $0.0885 to $0.0566. Interestingly, bulls have been defending this level even at the height of intense selling pressure.

So, if the support holds, a rebound towards the mid-range around $0.074 may follow. Otherwise, if the memecoin breaks the zone, $0.04 will be the next area where buyers could return.

First of all, Dogecoin ETFs have been inactive for the past month for the two products that are live in the U.S. The last activity was on 13th October, when it saw $138.57K in net outflows.

Over a period of one year, the ETF has had a cumulative net inflow of just $15 million despite being the king of all memes. These figures imply that its ETF interest has been muted.

That’s not all either as Hyperliquid longs have been heavily underwater too, with their average entry price on Dogecoin at $0.0842. This entry price seemed to be 28.41% above the press time price of the memecoin, hinting that a similar phenomenon was reflected in the derivative markets.

The $0.0842 level is now acting as dynamic resistance. If bulls can reclaim it, then it would serve as support.

The significant declines in prices suggested that long positions may be exposed to downside risk. In fact, there appeared to be large, long liquidation clusters at the $0.061 and $0.03-levels, adding to the selling pressure of the existing one.

Therefore, if DOGE can defend the support at $0.060 and absorb leveraged selling, a recovery would be feasible. Otherwise, the memecoin may break down and expose $0.04 or even lower demand levels.

Home » Ripple (XRP) » XRP Backer Counters SWIFT’s Latest Speed Report.

The preference for nearly-immediate settlement time windows unites a roster of banks in SWIFT’s chain trial.

A Swift report highlighting faster cross-border payments drew a pointed response from Digital Asset Investor, who replied that he prefers 3-4 seconds and pointed to XRP.

The exchange underscores the ongoing contrast between improvements in traditional interbank messaging and the settlement times associated with blockchain-based rails.

Swift’s Spotlight on Speed report, released this week, shows that 50% of payments on its network now reach the recipient institution within 40 seconds, with 75% arriving within 10 minutes.

According to recent reports, what will define the next generation of cross-border payments?The answer? More than just speed.Throughout @Sibos, conversations repeatedly focused on the customer experience. How do we make cross-border transactions more intuitive, more transparent and more predictable for… pic.twitter.com/yZoeZMDN4z.

The cooperative noted that these figures put the industry ahead of the G20’s target for one-hour end-to-end processing by 2027 in the interbank leg of the journey.

The same report emphasizes that the “last mile”, the period after a payment reaches the receiving bank and before it is credited to the beneficiary’s account, still accounts for about 80% of the average end-to-end journey time.

Across 40 receiving markets analyzed, median last-mile processing sat near one hour in roughly one-third of cases, with wide variation between cross-border markets.

The conglomerate has called for greater use of one-leg-out models that connect international payments to domestic instant systems to reduce those final delays.

Sources indicate that digital Asset Investor’s reply to the Swift post was brief: “I prefer 3-4 seconds. XRP.” The comment references the XRP Ledger’s typical ledger close time of roughly 3-5 seconds, which provides finality for on-ledger transfers.

In a recent development, I prefer 3-4 seconds. XRP. https://t.co/tBqXtEsqeM.

In Ripple’s On-Demand Liquidity (ODL) model, XRP is used as a bridge asset so that currency conversion and settlement can occur without pre-funded nostro accounts.

End-to-end ODL flows that include exchange conversions have been described in the 3-5 second range for the core ledger step, though real-world completion including compliance and local payouts is often measured in seconds to a few minutes depending on the corridor.

Recent findings suggest that the two claims are not measuring identical segments of a payment. Swift’s 40-second figure tracks time to the recipient institution, while the longer last-mile delays occur after that point.

https://t.co/ZA3CcggMOf @swiftcommunity @XRP @realfrandeolza @Archie_XRPL.

XRP’s cited 3-4 second window refers primarily to ledger settlement of the bridge asset itself.

Traditional systems still handle the bulk of global bank-to-bank volume and benefit from established compliance and messaging standards; blockchain rails emphasize reduced pre-funding and faster finality on the asset transfer.

Whether the shorter settlement window on XRP produces a meaningfully better end-user experience continues to depend on how the on- and off-ramps, local banking rails, and compliance steps are integrated in any given corridor.

XRP Ledger Foundation Director of Community Hussein Zangana (Vet) shared a tidbit of XRPL's early history in a recent X post.

Vet noted that the XRP Ledger (XRPL) still carries traces of Satoshi Nakamoto’s original Bitcoin design, highlighting two features.

According to recent reports, in 2011, three engineers—David Schwartz, Jed McCaleb, and Arthur Britto—began developing the XRP Ledger (XRPL). Fascinated by Bitcoin, they set out to create a better version that improved upon its limitations—with the goal of creating a digital asset that was more sustainable and built specifically for payments.

As reported, the first line of code for the core of what would become the XRP Ledger (XRPL) was written by David Schwartz, who is Ripple CTO emeritus, about 15 years ago, on November 11, 2011.

Vet delves into the earliest part of XRP Ledger history, noting that 15 years ago, the XRP Ledger started out using some Bitcoin code, including helper functions from the Bitcoin client that Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, wrote. Vet added that Jed McCaleb also copied Satoshi’s timekeeping code into the XRPL, even including one of the Bitcoin creator’s comments shared as a screenshot.

Did you know all of us on the XRP Ledger use design choices by Satoshi daily? 15 years ago, the XRP Ledger started out using some Bitcoin code, including helper functions from the Bitcoin client that Satoshi wrote. Jed copied Satoshi's timekeeping code into the XRPL, including one of Satoshi's comments. By the end of 2014, the original Satoshi code was gone. In December 2014, Nik Bougalis removed the last of the timekeeping code, along with Satoshi's comment. Two design choices of Satoshi still remain on the XRPL and all of us use at least one of it. Signature curve secp256k1 (we also support Ed25519 thus not everyone uses this) and how XRPL addresses are generated from the public key with SHA-256 followed by RIPEMD-160, that's what all of us use.

The quote "Never go to sea with two chronometers; take one or three" is a classic maritime adage famously included by Satoshi Nakamoto (the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin) within the Bitcoin source code.

Sources indicate that vet explained that by the end of 2014, the original Satoshi code was gone from the XRP Ledger. In December 2014, former Ripple engineering lead Nik Bougalis removed the last of the timekeeping code, along with Satoshi's comment.

In a recent development, however, two of Satoshi's design choices still remain on the XRP Ledger: the first is the secp256k1 signature curve, which Bitcoin uses and which the XRP Ledger continues to support. However, the ledger also supports Ed25519, meaning not every XRPL user relies on secp256k1.

"I remember David saying they used secp256k1 so no one would doubt the security because it's the same as Bitcoin's, etc.," Vet stated, citing the insight of the Ripple CTO emeritus on secp256k1, adding, "Lots of interesting things to dig into from the early days.".

The second is the method used to generate XRP Ledger addresses from public keys. The process applies SHA-256 hashing followed by RIPEMD-160, a design inherited from Bitcoin that remains common to all XRPL addresses.

Asked why the timekeeping code and Satoshi's comment were removed, Vet explained that this became leftover code as newly introduced code was introduced, so it was cleaned up.

Cardano DReps have rejected a proposal by Toto Finance to spend 22 million ADA from the Cardano treasury on a "Strategic Copper Reserve.".

The vote closed on Nov. 15, and DReps holding 2.86 billion ADA voted against the proposal, according to Cardano governance data. DReps with 20.02 million ADA voted in favor of it.

DRep John MacPherson was among those who voted "No," and he explained his decision in a post on X.

MacPherson wrote that he is not against real-world assets on Cardano. Still, he said the proposal asks the treasury "to take on both the copper price and the ada price," and Toto Finance would collect "up to about 3.4M ada in fees.".

At the same time, MacPherson noted that the proposal is “more honest about its risks than most.”.

Industry observers note that toto Finance, a company led by Monty Metzger, submitted the proposal on Oct. 15. ADA is trading at $0.152 on Monday, and the requested 22 million ADA is now worth around $3.3 million.

The initiative was to buy copper with 14.72 million ADA and store it in a warehouse near Fresh Orleans. Toto Finance wanted to issue one CuTT token for each pound of copper. The metal would be sold in 18 to 24 months.

The Cardano Foundation, which votes as a DRep, announced its "No" vote in October.

"We recognize the opportunity in real-world asset tokenization; however, this proposal places 22,000,000 ada under the recipient's sole control to fund a fee-heavy concentrated commodity position whose safeguards are not yet in place," the foundation wrote.

Three members of the Constitutional Committee voted "No," and the other four members did not vote.

Crypto commentator Ingeniero Cripto agreed with MacPherson in the replies under his post. He called the "double exposure" to the prices of copper and ADA the key problem of the proposal, as the Cardano treasury already holds ADA.

According to him, RWAs on Cardano make sense, but “funding the asset itself is a different question than funding the rails.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alaska is yet to be called, but the writing is on the wall for President Donald Trump and the Republican Party. The Democrats have seized control of both the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House of Representatives.

For all intents and purposes, this means that Trump is now a lame duck president.

Industry observers note that that’s the least of his worries, though, as Democrats could now set their sights on investigating Trump’s crypto ventures. After all, this is a man who amassed a fortune of close to $1.5 billion from cryptocurrency ventures in the first year of his second term in office.

Donald Trump became the first sitting president to launch a memecoin, with OFFICIAL TRUMP [TRUMP] generating over $600M in licensing fees and royalties alone. All while a majority of the memecoin’s retail investors saw red.

He is also the “Co-Founder Emeritus” of World Liberty Financial [WLFI], a DeFi and cryptocurrency platform. According to public filings, the project, co-founded by Eric Trump, Barron Trump, and Donald Trump Jr., brought in $799M in 2025 alone.

It has been revealed that then there’s the matter of an Abu Dhabi-based fund buying $2 billion in USD1, WLF’s own stablecoin, to invest in Binance after the crypto exchange was fined over $4 billion for money laundering violations. Its founder, Changpeng Zhao, pled guilty and served a 4-month jail term before being pardoned by Trump.

Recent findings suggest that simply put, it can be argued that the president has used his position (and crypto) to monetize the presidency and enrich his personal fortune. Hence, the investigations.

Moving ahead, what should the industry expect now that the Democrats are in control of the U.S Congress?

In a recent development, well, it wouldn’t be unreasonable to expect a gridlock. After all, many in the crypto industry have historically backed Republican candidates because they championed free market de-regulation and digital asset frameworks.

On the contrary, several prominent Democrats like Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is also expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, have often been vocal critics of the sector.

Sources indicate that however, expecting the worst outcome possible here would allude to a very superficial reading of the situation. This is why it’s crucial to differentiate between what will happen, what can happen, and what won’t happen.

Yes, the likes of Warren haven’t been the most receptive towards the sector, but party-wide support has been growing over the years.

Consider this – following the latest midterm elections, there are a total of 50 pro-crypto senators against just 33 anti-crypto ones. Similarly, in the House, 241 are at the moment pro-crypto as opposed to 104 who are against crypto.

Those are significant numbers. More importantly, they also suggest that despite some historical bias, the sector enjoys some degree of bipartisan support.

Recent findings suggest that the example of Fairshake is a case in point. The Crypto Super PAC spent millions backing 33 House candidates during the midterms. 19 Republicans and 14 Democrats. At the time of writing, 29 of them had already won.

Recent findings suggest that legislative evidence from before the midterms is worth looking at too. As Andrew Nalichaev, CEO of HAIA Finance, pointed out,.

Recent findings suggest that … support for rules concerning stablecoins has received bipartisan backing: the GENIUS Act passed the Senate 68 to 30 and the House 308 to 122. An key issue that led to the failure of the CLARITY Act in September was the ethics issue regarding officials involved in issuing or supporting tokens.

Likewise, Luke Jacobi, Founder and Editor at OptimistFi, told AMBCrypto,.

Recent findings suggest that our small comparison of two House final-passage votes on July 17, 2025 found that 102 of 212 voting Democrats backed GENIUS, compared with 78 of 212 for CLARITY: 48.1% versus 36.8%. Both attracted cross-party support, but the 24-vote difference demonstrates why a single ‘pro-crypto’ label misses policy-specific disagreement.

According to a recent report, over 30% of the population, or 70M people, now hold digital assets. It is evidence that despite some skepticism and vocal criticism, the industry has reached a level of financial integration that will be difficult to reverse right now.

It has been revealed that it is also evidence that crypto is no longer a single-party issue. Both red and blue states have their own share of crypto holders. In time, their numbers will grow, and so will the degree of bipartisan support the industry enjoys from lawmakers.

In a recent development, however, the concerns about a possible legislative gridlock and its potential impact on the regulatory clarity the industry desperately seeks aren’t totally unwarranted. In the current landscape, Democrats control the U.S. Congress, while Republicans control the White House.

And while he did suggest that he looks forward to working with Democrats, President Trump has also asserted that he will wield his veto power if need be, especially since Democrats don’t enjoy a veto-proof or filibuster-proof majority.

This means that realistically, we can expect a certain level of gridlock across the board ranging from budgets, appropriations, and defense spending. Even crypto, if the fresh U.S. Congress is intent on investigating President Trump’s ventures.

Sources indicate that hence, the question: How significant a concern could this be? According to Dmitri Mihhailov, General Partner at Prifinance,.

Investigations do not change laws already on the books, and the most key one for the industry is already there – The GENIUS Act.

Mihhailov also told AMBCrypto that in his view,.

… gridlock hurts what is still missing: a federal framework for crypto trading markets. Until Congress passes one, firms rely on agency guidance and court rulings, and a future SEC or CFTC can change guidance much more easily than a statute.

In fact, it can be argued that it’s not the investigation itself that could be concerning for the crypto-sector. Instead, it’s the calendar that could be the problem. Especially since congressional investigations consume time, staff, resources, and political capital, all of which can be used to pass necessary crypto legislation.

The “Wild West.” That’s the reputation the cryptocurrency industry had once upon a time.

Industry observers note that gone are those days, though, as the sector became more mainstream and was embraced by institutions and people world over. Banks, lawmakers, and even nation-states. Heck, even Trump did that within years of calling Bitcoin “a scam.”.

Sources indicate that politics is a fickle game, though. It’s not unreasonable to contemplate that some legislators could turn on the industry if the congressional investigations into Trump’s crypto ventures go underway.

Industry observers note that the thing is, as an industry, crypto has well and truly arrived on the world stage over the last few years. Despite perceptions, it is too substantial to be defined by a singular person’s business interests. In fact, more than political scrutiny, THAT would be the biggest threat to the sector.

As IronWallet’s Ermo Eero put it,.

According to recent reports, the danger is that crypto as a whole becomes politically coded through its association with high-profile ventures like memecoins and politically connected stablecoins. If every crypto vote starts to look like a vote on a specific politician, moderates on both sides will find it easier to abstain or delay.

Then what could these investigations yield? Well, at the very least, clear-cut ethics, disclosures, and conflict of interest rules for public officials – proposals that were at the core of the CLARITY Act’s failure. And, at the end of the day, won’t that be a win for the industry as a whole?

So, no. While there might be some distancing, lawmakers won’t turn on crypto.

Industry observers note that 2026 hasn’t been a great year for the crypto sector so far. The markets aren’t exactly booming, billions have been lost to hacks, and the CLARITY Act failed to go through. Plus, the current President of the United States could soon find himself at the center of an investigation into his crypto dealings.

The midterm election results are not.

It is simply a matter of getting used to the new balance of power in Washington D.C.

Yi He, the co-founder of the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, has sparked discussions across the crypto market after urging retail traders to stay calm even as major crypto assets continue to post massive daily losses.

Yi He’s consoling statement has come as crypto traders grow increasingly weary and the prolonged market volatility begins to cause even bigger losses, with Bitcoin retesting $63,000.

In her post, Yi urged investors holding major crypto assets that have been substantially affected by the severe market volatility to remain calm amid the latest market downturn.

She described the ongoing crypto market pullback as ‘temporary’ while assuring spot traders that they have little reason to worry.

Alongside the post, Yi He shared a link to the Binance app showcasing a 30-day asset change of approximately -$101.31 million in her account.

The figure indicates the amount of losses the pro-crypto investor has suffered on her holdings over a period of about a month, from October 17 to November 16, 2026.

Although the showcased portfolio reveals a decline in the founder’s holdings, it does not establish whether the decline represents realized trading losses, unrealized losses, withdrawals, or other changes in Yi He’s account.

It appears that some investors may have found comfort in Yi He's message as they expressed support, noting that turbulent conditions like these don’t necessarily last long.

However, other commentators have questioned whether wealthy industry figures like Yi He can fully understand the financial pressure facing retail traders at a time like this.

Some of the arguments questioned how meaningful such reassurance could be for retail investors, arguing that losing 100 million yuan might not significantly affect someone with substantial wealth like her.

Meanwhile, a loss of 20,000 or 30,000 yuan could wipe out an ordinary investor's savings.

Will Aave’s $21M bet on Bitcoin’s lending potential restore DeFi liquidity or create newly introduced risk?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ambcrypto

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that with over 4% of USDT supply being removed in Q4, worth around $10 billion, there is still not enough dry powder to confirm that the market has hit bottom.
  • In essence, could this be the much needed catalyst for a DeFi resurgence?
  • In a recent development, Aave [AAVE] has gained DAO approval to add support for using Bitcoin as collateral.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the main metrics to look at is liquidity.

It has been revealed that with over 4% of USDT supply being removed in Q4, worth around $10 billion, there is still not enough dry powder to confirm that the market has hit bottom. In this context, Aave’s decision to allow Bitcoin to be used within DeFi lending becomes a lot more impactful. Naturally, the question becomes — Can the move increase capital inflows by allowing consumers to use Bitcoin as collateral and therefore increase stablecoin volumes?

In essence, could this be the much needed catalyst for a DeFi resurgence?

In a recent development, Aave [AAVE] has gained DAO approval to add support for using Bitcoin as collateral.

The proposal will allow holders to lock up their BTC to borrow stablecoins. Notably, the proposal was unanimously approved on 9th November. This means Bitcoin holders can gain fresh liquidity through Aave’s $21 million credit market by borrowing stablecoins using their BTC as collateral.

In a recent development, as the chart below demonstrates, Aave will be allocating $21 million to their credit products to five different stablecoins. The two largest stablecoins will be USDT and USDC which have been allocated $8 million each. These account for almost 76% of the total capacity.

Meanwhile, AAVE’s native stablecoin GHO will be allocated $1 million. The last $4 million will be split evenly between USDG and RLUSD with $2 million allocated to each.

Why does this matter? Well, this allocation highlights that Aave is looking to blend both traditional stablecoins and newer assets to provide more options for borrowing. Consequently, this will allow Bitcoin holders to borrow against several stablecoin markets using their BTC as collateral.

As Aave Founder and CEO Stani Kulechov explained,.

In a recent development, the Babylon-built Bitcoin-backed market on Aave V4 highlights how easily newly introduced markets can be launched using the Hub and Spoke model. Native BTC collateral, without wrappers or custodians, unlocks a major new source of liquidity for on-chain borrowing and lending.

Crypto lending is slowing down as borrowers reduce their exposure amid market uncertainty.

According to recent reports, according to Galaxy Research, the overall crypto-backed loan market fell by 16.78% during Q2, hitting a total value of $56.16 billion. This is the first time that all major lending sectors have fallen since 2022. DeFi lending also saw a sharp fall, with total active loans decreasing from $47.13 billion to $21.94 billion between April and July. In short, traders have lost interest in borrowing against their assets.

Recent findings suggest that however, Aave has seen an opposite trend, with the platform noting all-time highs in active loans on the Aave V4 platform, increasing by almost 100% in Q2 to $500 million. Against this backdrop, the addition of Bitcoin to the lending market could lend further growth potential.

In essence, by allowing BTC holders to use their asset as collateral, the market could see more capital flowing into DeFi, more collateral on Aave, and more demand for on-chain borrowing.

Aave V4’s Hub-and-Spoke architecture provides an isolated environment in which integrations can deploy both standard and custom Spokes without affecting other assets on the Hub.

The crypto market is facing its worst liquidity crunch since the 2022 bear market.

The overall stablecoin market cap has fallen by about $14 billion over the past month. By 10th November, the total stablecoin market cap was around $290 billion, according to DeFiLlama. In fact, the last two weeks alone saw the most net stablecoin outflows ever in over four years. Over half of this drop came from USDT and a further 20% from USDC.

It has been revealed that this pressure can be seen across the DeFi space. In fact, the total DeFi TVL fell to around $76.6 billion on 12th November, with stablecoin market cap sitting at $286.9 billion at press time. However, DeFi TVL also fell by 9.7% week-on-week.

Against this backdrop, Aave’s move could offer a new source of liquidity.

According to recent reports, there is one technical distinction worth keeping though. This integration doesn’t automatically mean any new stablecoins will flow into DeFi. Instead, borrowers will have access to liquidity that is already sitting in Aave. For liquidity to grow, the protocol will also need to attract more lenders and fresh deposits.

As per the attached chart, there is still a long way to go before the lending market on Bitcoin hits significant levels.

BTC-backed loans reached $3.58 billion in 2025, representing just 0.24% of Bitcoin’s market cap. So, by supporting Bitcoin as collateral, Aave could help unlock this largely untapped lending demand.

Aave’s move could also expose its lending market to greater risks.

According to recent reports, according to AMBCrypto, although this latest borrowing opportunity on Aave will create new demand, it can also lead to greater speculation. Customers can borrow stablecoins using BTC as collateral and then re-lend them into leveraged crypto positions.

Consider this — Bitcoin Futures Open Interest increased by 12.1% in 19 days up to late-October, despite a 5.3% price decrease in BTC. This indicated that traders were increasing their leveraged exposure.

This continued into November, with Bitfinex reporting that this was the fifth time traders added leverage to their positions while BTC fell. The previous 4 times this occurred, traders executed liquidations of long positions worth over $800 million.

For Aave, the concern is that easier access to Bitcoin credit could add another source of speculation.

Ultimately, the move by Aave to integrate Bitcoin comes at a time where DeFi needs liquidity. However, its impact remains to be seen still. While the integration could entice early lenders and stablecoin deposits, there is a risk that high levels of demand could come from speculation and cause further volatility in the market.

Industry observers note that thus, Aave may unlock a fresh source of liquidity. However, turning that liquidity into DeFi growth will be the test.

#5850. Banxa’s Shaun Heng Warns Rapid Fintech Growth Can Conceal Hidden Risks

Banxa’s Shaun Heng Warns Rapid Fintech Growth Can Conceal Hidden Risks

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2260 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailycoin

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Home » Interviews » Banxa’s Shaun Heng Warns Rapid Fintech Growth Can Conceal Hidden Risks.
  • An interview with Banxa’s Chief Product & Growth Officer on hidden scaling traps and the future of stablecoin payments.
  • Industry observers note that rapid growth is often seen as a sign of success in fintech.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home » Interviews » Banxa’s Shaun Heng Warns Rapid Fintech Growth Can Conceal Hidden Risks.

An interview with Banxa’s Chief Product & Growth Officer on hidden scaling traps and the future of stablecoin payments.

Industry observers note that rapid growth is often seen as a sign of success in fintech. But as transaction volumes increase, weaknesses in payment infrastructure, fraud prevention and risk management can become harder to spot – and more costly to fix.

Recent findings suggest that shaun Heng, Chief Product & Growth Officer at Banxa, a global crypto payments infrastructure provider, knows these challenges firsthand. Before joining Banxa, Heng held product and growth leadership roles at MoonPay and CoinMarketCap, gaining experience across two major players in the digital asset space.

In this interview with DailyCoin, he discusses why rapid growth can expose hidden vulnerabilities in fintech, what it takes to build payment infrastructure that works at scale, and how stablecoins could reshape the future of global payments.

– When does rapid growth become a risk for fintech companies?

Our total transaction volume (TTV) grew 76% from January to August. Stablecoins increased by 117%. Great numbers. The first thing I asked was where they came from?

Growth becomes a risk signal the moment it outruns the systems underneath it. That happens more often than people admit.

When volume doubles, every weakness doubles with it. That could mean fraud attempts, chargeback exposure, reconciliation breaks. Just to name a few. So you’re always looking at a great number next to problems that may not have appeared yet.

Sources indicate that the second challenge is that fast growth is almost never evenly distributed. It could be one particular partner, region, digital asset, or payment method. That concentration is invisible on a topline chart, so we always look deeper to understand the drivers and future success.

It has been revealed that and team culture is real. In a quarter everyone has worked so hard and exceeded targets, nobody wants to be the one asking hard questions.

The discipline I would push for is simple: break down the growth before you celebrate it. Where is it coming from? Which rails is it riding on? And what happens if one of those rails is withdrawn next week?

Growth becomes a risk signal the moment it outruns the systems underneath it.

– What does a payment infrastructure provider need to deliver to make the crypto on-ramp experience seamless?

For a long time the industry shipped widgets, and a widget is a visible admission that someone else is handling this.

Banxa Native is headless by design. The partner owns the interface, the brand, the pricing presentation, the whole journey. We simply sit behind their stack. Users never.

Returning owners never verify twice, because existing KYC can be reused through token sharing. So, everything the user shouldn’t have to think about. That’s the definition of invisible.

In practice, it means the provider owns licensing, or a licensed local partner, in every market where money actually moves,  local payment methods, not just cards, because owners pay the way their country pays.

Vietnam is the example I keep reaching for. We launched VietQR there in Q3, and it is already our top payment method in that region at roughly 42% of all transactions — driving a conversion rate close to eight times higher than cards. Same owners, same product, same pricing. The only variable was letting people pay the way they already pay.

Then provider also need identity and KYC, including the ability to accept verification the partner has already done. Settlement, in and out, with money arriving where it is supposed to on the day it is supposed to.

It has been revealed that and it has to run in both directions, not just the buy flow. On-ramp, where a user pays with a local method and receives crypto. Off-ramp, where they sell and cashout to their own bank account.

A lot of products ship the first and treat off-ramp as a secondary problem, and that is precisely the moment a user discovers the money only moves one way.

Sources indicate that for a European fintech, Banxa collects the local payment, exchanges and settles the fiat leg where the partner needs it. We carry the MiCA licence that passports across the EU — so they don’t have to build a crypto licensing and payments stack country by country.

Recent findings suggest that one partner, one compliance review, one integration, both directions. That speed to market is usually why partners choose us.

It has been revealed that – Banxa’s infrastructure supports stablecoin payments across B2B settlement, consumer payments, and cross-border transactions. What is the most overlooked challenge in making stablecoin payments work at scale?

Nobody has ever been excited about reconciliation, and it is the thing that decides whether you have a business.

Sources indicate that A stablecoin transfer settles in seconds. That part is genuinely solved.

Industry observers note that what is not solved is everything around it. The fiat leg still moves on banking hours and local scheme rules. You have a bank partner on one side, a chain on the other, and a treasury position sitting between them that has to be funded, hedged and accounted for.

Every transaction has to be matched across those systems, in the right currency, on the right day, with the right fee breakdown, in a form an auditor and a regulator will accept.

The second unglamorous thing is failure handling.

At scale, the interesting work is not the happy path. It is the payment that half-completes.

It has been revealed that the most common example is card decline and for many reasons – bank limit, 3D Secure step that timed out etc. In most checkouts that ends the order and the buyer needs to start again, or more often leaves.

Then there are bank transfers that arrive three days late with a truncated reference. The refund that has to go back to a card when the crypto has already left.

Users judge you almost entirely on how those cases are handled, and those cases are where most providers quietly fall over.

We recently shipped Payment Method Switch, which lets the buyer change how they pay without losing the order. It separates the order from the payment, so a buyer can move from card to Google Pay without losing the order or redoing verification, and so they see the latest method before confirming.

The third challenge is payment method coverage, which sounds like a commercial checklist and is actually an engineering and licensing dependency.

In a recent development, supporting the way people pay in the US, Nigeria, Australia and Germany means four different integrations, four different fraud profiles and four different regulatory conversations. A switch only works if the alternative payment method is already connected and live for that buyer.

It has been revealed that it matters because this is the layer the user is trusting without knowing it. When the plumbing is right, the experience feels effortless. When it is wrong, it does not feel like a backend problem. It feels like the product lied to them.

– Can KYC be more than compliance — can it actually become a growth advantage in crypto payments?

Industry observers note that yes, and I would go further. KYC is one of the highest-leverage product surfaces in payments. Most teams just never treat it as one.

Industry observers note that look at where users actually drop. It is rarely pricing. It is the verification step.

Recent findings suggest that someone has decided they want to transact, they have intent, and then they are asked to photograph a document on a screen that does not match the app they were just in. A meaningful share of them never come back.

According to recent reports, that is not a compliance cost. That is a conversion problem.

So the advantage comes from three things.

First, verify once. If a partner has already verified a user to a standard we can rely on, that user should not be asked again. Banxa Native supports exactly this through token sharing, so returning consumers go straight to payment.

Sources indicate that second, verify proportionately. Not every transaction carries the same risk, so it shouldn’t carry the same friction.

Sources indicate that third, verify natively. No redirect, no third-party screen, no moment where the user wonders who they just handed their passport details to.

According to recent reports, there is a trust argument too. In most of the world, people are more willing to move money with a platform that looks regulated, not less. Verification done well signals that this is a real financial product. Done badly, suggests the opposite.

My advice is to instrument it. Measure drop-off by step. Iterate. Most teams hand it to engineering once and never look again.

– Crypto payments come with a lot of risk, from payment disputes to fraud. Do you the industry underestimates the value of having someone else take on that risk?

It has been revealed that badly, yes. And the reason is that the cost of carrying it yourself does not show up as a line item until it is already a problem.

The fiat leg is reversible. The crypto leg is not. A card payment can be disputed months after the asset has left. That gap is where fraud lives.

According to recent reports, so when a platform decides to run its own ramp, they’re usually pricing the integration work. What they are not pricing is the loss rate, the rules engine that has to keep up with it, the team watching it at three in the morning, the bank relationships that get withdrawn when your chargeback ratio crosses a threshold, and the capital you have to hold against all of it.

Those costs are lumpy and they arrive late.

According to recent reports, the real value of transferring that risk is not just the losses avoided. It is focus.

According to recent reports, with Banxa Native, the partner owns the experience end to end. We carry the regulated rails and the settlement behind it. They get to spend their engineering time on the things their users actually chose them for.

Risk you have not priced is still risk. Someone is carrying it.

– What’s one thing Web3 companies still see as “just compliance” that should really be treated as a product or growth problem?

Market access. Which licences you hold, and therefore which countries you can actually serve, is usually filed under legal. It is the single biggest determinant of your addressable market.

Sources indicate that teams spend enormous effort on acquisition and then discover the funnel is geographically capped. Users arrive, get to the payment step, and find out their country is not supported or their local payment method is not available.

It has been revealed that from the user’s point of view, the product simply does not work. From the growth team’s point of view, the conversion rate is mysteriously bad in half the world. Nobody connects that back to a licensing decision made two years earlier.

Industry observers note that the same is true of regulatory readiness ahead of a regime change. MiCA is the clearest recent example.

According to recent reports, the companies that treated it as a legal deadline scrambled. The ones that treated it as a product decision kept serving European users without interruption while others paused service. Continuity of access is a growth outcome.

Sources indicate that this is also why we think about our licence footprint as product surface area rather than paperwork. Banxa services users across North America, Europe, the UK, Latin America and Asia-Pacific, and is MiCA-authorised as a CASP in the Netherlands. For a partner building on Banxa, that footprint is not a compliance appendix in the contract. It is the list of countries where their product works.

My general rule: if a compliance decision changes who can use your product or how easily, it was never only a compliance decision.

– What development in crypto payments could have the biggest impact on the industry over the next few years?

Stablecoins becoming the default settlement layer for ordinary businesses that have no interest in crypto.

It has been revealed that that is the shift. It isn’t necessarily about more people buying digital assets. It’s about companies moving money across borders faster and cheaper, with the stablecoin being an implementation detail they never discuss.

Sources indicate that the future isn’t crypto payments. It’s better payments.

The numbers say it is already happening.

Stablecoin supply has actually contracted since May, from around $310 billion to roughly $286 billion. But payment volume went the other way. Allium reported it at $482 billion in the first nine months of this year, up 45% year on year.

Banks, card networks and large fintechs are integrating this into their products right now.

What makes it transformative is the disappearance, not the technology.

Consumers will keep using the apps and currencies they already trust. The rails underneath will change. Identity handled once, not repeatedly. Settlement in minutes instead of days. Fees people can actually see.

In many emerging markets, this will go further and faster than people in Washington or London expect, because the alternative is genuinely slow.

Digital dollars become the practical choice for savings and cross-border flows, not a theoretical one.

Sources indicate that most customers will never know a stablecoin was involved. That’s the point.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that solana has officially removed the "beta" tag from its mainnet's name and introduced the Solana 1.0 standard. The switch was declared on Nov. 16 at the Breakpoint conference in London.

"Solana 1.0 marks the network's graduation from 'mainnet beta' to 'mainnet,' retiring the beta designation it has carried since launch," the Solana Foundation said.

Solana launched on March 16, 2020, and the network had been working under the "mainnet-beta" label for six years and eight months. According to the foundation, the label "never evolved to signal its production status.".

According to recent reports, the Solana Foundation coordinated the rollout with the Anza and Firedancer teams. Co-founder Anatoly Yakovenko replied to the announcement on X with three exploding-head emojis.

In a recent development, "For users, this is the same network, nothing changes. Your SOL, accounts, assets, applications, and transaction history remain the same," the foundation wrote. On Monday, SOL is trading at $71.35.

It has been revealed that according to the foundation, two upgrades made the change possible. In October, Solana activated Alpenglow with the Agave 4.3 release, and the time to final confirmation went down by almost 99%, from 12.8 seconds to around 150 milliseconds.

Firedancer, a validator client developed by Jump Crypto independently from Agave, is also now running on the Solana mainnet. Independent implementations "limit the impact of bugs affecting one client, and strengthen network resilience," the foundation said.

Solana 1.0 also gives the network a shared protocol version, and it does not depend on the version numbers of individual clients such as Agave and Firedancer.

"A shared protocol version lets everyone refer to Solana's evolution without using one client's release number as shorthand for the entire network," the Solana Foundation explained. "Announcing a protocol version does not activate every associated improvement at once.".

Earlier this year, Solana raised the compute limit per block from 60 million to 100 million compute units in May, and the slot time went down from 400 to 200 milliseconds in August. The maximum transaction size also went up from 1,232 to 4,096 bytes.

"Documentation, websites, explorers, and other ecosystem surfaces will progressively reflect the updated designation," the foundation added.

Home » Esports » Project Helix Xbox Console Will Run PC Games: What It Means for Web3.

Microsoft VP Jason Ronald details how the next-gen console merges Xbox libraries with PC gaming.

Microsoft has officially clarified its vision for the upcoming Project Helix Xbox console, confirming in the Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine that the next-generation system is built to run both traditional Xbox libraries and PC games. A hybrid shift could also open upcoming doors for Web3 gaming.

As Microsoft celebrates Xbox’s 25th anniversary, the company has shared fresh architectural details about the Project Helix Xbox console, its upcoming next-generation console. When Microsoft first introduced the project earlier this year, it confirmed that the new system would bring Xbox and PC gaming closer together. This led many to assume that Helix would essentially be a Windows gaming PC packaged in a console design.

In a four-page Q&A inside the Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine, Vice President of Next Generation Jason Ronald pushed back directly against that framing.

Recent findings suggest that “Project Helix is designed to be a console capable of playing games from your PC,” Ronald stated. “It is not a PC that can also play console games.”.

For Microsoft, the distinction comes down to removing the friction traditionally associated with PC gaming, such as driver management, multiple launchers, and complex configuration menus, while keeping deeper controls accessible for enthusiasts.

It has been revealed that “The goal is making it easy, intuitive, and instant to access my games,” Ronald explained. “But if you’re a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customizability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go do it.”.

According to Ronald and the anniversary feature, Project Helix is being built around several core pillars:.

Project Helix, which Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has previously described as a broader “family of devices” rather than a single box, is taking shape during a turbulent stretch for Microsoft’s gaming division.

After taking the helm earlier in 2026, Sharma oversaw major restructuring, studio closures, and layoffs, candidly remarking in July that the Xbox brand was “not healthy.” Simultaneously, ongoing global memory and storage component shortages have pushed up manufacturing costs across the hardware industry, prompting some players to urge both Microsoft and Sony to delay next-gen launches until prices stabilize.

Ronald acknowledged those supply-chain headwinds, calling the current hardware environment “brutal,” though he argued that the constraints are forcing Xbox engineers to innovate rather than simply throw costlier components at the machine.

Microsoft has not revealed a price or consumer launch window for Project Helix, though alpha developer hardware is slated to begin shipping in 2027, with retail speculation pointing toward late 2027 or 2028.

For the Web3 gaming sector, Microsoft’s hybrid console-PC strategy could solve a long-standing distribution bottleneck.

Historically, console manufacturers have enforced strict platform policies against blockchain integrations, external crypto wallets, and NFTs, forcing Web3 studios to build almost exclusively for PC, web browsers, and mobile devices.

Still, Ronald noted that the ROG Xbox Ally served as a testing ground for unifying game libraries across multiple stores.

If Project Helix eventually supports third-party PC storefronts such as Steam and the Epic Games Store, it could create fresh opportunities for blockchain-enabled games to reach console audiences.

In a recent development, however, important questions remain unanswered. Microsoft has not confirmed third-party storefront support on Project Helix, nor has it unveiled native support for external crypto wallets, NFT functionality, or blockchain transactions.

Nevertheless, the direction is worth watching. If Project Helix successfully bridges the console and PC gaming ecosystems, it could create newly introduced distribution opportunities for Web3 games and help bring blockchain-powered gaming experiences closer to mainstream players.

The sixth-generation Ford Mustang Shelby GT350 was an enthusiast’s favorite. It offered a track-ready middle ground between the standard V-8-powered GT and the supercharged Shelby GT500, with a 5.2-liter naturally aspirated “Voodoo” V-8 pumping out 526 horsepower and revving to 8250 rpm, and a 6-speed manual transmission. The GT350 left production in 2020; Ford has not replaced it with a like-for-like variant for in the current seventh-generation Mustang lineup. But that could change as soon as next year.

Ford Authority is reporting that Ford sent out dealer documents confirming a new high-performance Mustang. The new Mustang would not be called the Shelby GT350—Ford has not used Shelby branding for the S650-generation Mustang, and Shelby American is currently building its own GT350. But the new model would, it seems, fulfill that role in the lineup. (Road & Track reached out to Ford for comment on the potential new Mustang, but a spokesperson only noted the brand “can’t comment on speculation” about future vehicles.).

It has been revealed that the report claims the upcoming Mustang would slot between the current Mustang Dark Horse and the Dark Horse SC, and would feature either a 5.2-liter or 5.4-liter naturally aspirated V-8. A six-speed manual transmission would be available, if not the only option, and the new Mustang—unlike the Dark Horse SC—would only be available as a coupe. Per the report, it would arrive in late 2027 as a 2028 model-year vehicle and have a limited production run through the 2029 model year.

Sources indicate that firm performance specs were not detailed for the potential newly introduced Mustang, but Ford Authority expects the power output to be around 600 hp, slotting between the 500-hp Mustang Dark Horse and the 795-hp Mustang Dark Horse SC. No word yet on pricing, either; however, the current Mustang lineup has a large gap between the $72,760 Dark Horse Premium and the $108,085 Dark Horse SC where this vehicle would fit in nicely.

Recent findings suggest that ford has been looking at options to “expand on the Mustang family,” with reported ideas including non-traditional variants such as a four-door coupe-style sedan and even an off-road variant. Reviving the manual GT350 Mustang, at least in spirit, would counter those sacrilegious notions with some welcome red meat for enthusiasts.

  • Sources indicate that deposits move at network speed, which also means there is no chargeback mechanism once a transaction confirms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canadian gamblers have spent the past two years quietly rerouting their deposits from Interac transfers and prepaid vouchers to Bitcoin wallets. The shift is practical, driven primarily by settlement speed. A bank e-transfer can sit in processing over a long weekend, while a BTC confirmation clears in roughly ten minutes regardless of province or statutory holiday. Searches for btc casinos and btc casino online have climbed accordingly, though the operators behind those results vary wildly in licensing, game fairness, and how seriously they treat withdrawal limits.

According to recent reports, roobet has built its reputation as the category’s reference point. Its BTC casino model skips fiat rails entirely, crediting deposits as soon as a transaction confirms on-chain rather than waiting for a payment processor to batch it overnight. That design choice is a major reason it keeps surfacing at the top of Canadian comparison lists, even against operators with longer track records.

Sources indicate that deposits move at network speed, which also means there is no chargeback mechanism once a transaction confirms. Players carry the volatility themselves between deposit and cashout, and a platform that converts to stablecoins at deposit removes that exposure in a way a straight BTC balance does not. The sector’s shift toward stablecoin settlement largely reflects players being burned by holding BTC through a losing session during a price drop. Withdrawal limits tell a similar story: a casino that caps daily cashouts low enough to slow a winning streak is usually managing its own liquidity risk. So people should be looking at the fine print on payout ceilings, which deserve more attention than the headline bonus.

Ranked side by side, the gap is less about game count and more about withdrawal friction and Canadian access.

According to recent reports, provably fair systems let a player verify, after the fact, that a game’s outcome wasn’t altered after they placed their bet, using a published seed and hash. It is a meaningful trust layer, but it only confirms a round wasn’t tampered with, not that the house edge is favorable. Canadian players comparing operators against real-money alternatives still need to check return-to-player rates game by game, since a verifiable algorithm and a generous payout rate are separate questions that marketing copy tends to blur.

It has been revealed that most offshore crypto casinos serving Canadians are licensed through the Kahnawake Gaming Commission, based in Mohawk Territory in Quebec, which has issued gambling licenses since 1999. Ontario is the exception: since April 2022 it has run its own regulated online market through iGaming Ontario, meaning operators without an Ontario registration are technically off-limits to residents there, even if the rest of the country can reach them freely. That patchwork is why “player protection” means something different depending on which province a deposit originates in.

Recent findings suggest that none of that structure fixes the harder problem: crypto deposits remove the natural friction that used to slow a losing streak. A platform worth using still publishes deposit limits and self-exclusion tools on the same page as its game lobby, not buried three clicks deep. That detail tells a player more about the platform’s integrity than any welcome offer does.

Japan's Cabinet Office reported in its first estimate on Nov. 16 that real GDP fell 0.1% at an annualized rate in July–September. The quarterly decline rounded to -0.0%, while private consumption fell 0.3% from the previous quarter. The annualized figure describes the quarterly pace expressed over a year, not a year-over-year fall.

The composition was mixed: domestic demand added 0.6 percentage point to quarterly growth, while net exports subtracted 0.6 point.

His personal caution coexists with the Bank's conditional stance of further rate increases as activity, prices and financial conditions develop, alongside upside inflation risks.

There is pressure in the other direction, too. In a Nov. 16 speech, board member Hajime Takata argued for nimbler tightening and described his October proposal for a 1.5% rate as his personal view. The Board had rejected that proposal.

Weak consumption strengthens the argument for patience, but inflation risk keeps further tightening in the policy debate. The GDP number alone cannot settle that tension.

It has been revealed that november 16 GDP adds a growth argument for caution. The existing BOJ target is 1.25%; Bitcoin transmission remains conditional.

64K Bitcoin Miners Hijacked: Why the Attack Failed to Shake BTC

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Home » Bitcoin (BTC) » 64K Bitcoin Miners Hijacked: Why the Attack Failed to Shake BTC.
  • An AI-assisted exploit of Luxor’s software briefly diverted 1.4% of Bitcoin’s global computing power.
  • An AI-assisted exploit of Luxor’s fleet-management software briefly diverted 1.4% of Bitcoin’s global computing power, netting the attacker over $10,500 while leaving the blockchain itself untouched.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home » Bitcoin (BTC) » 64K Bitcoin Miners Hijacked: Why the Attack Failed to Shake BTC.

An AI-assisted exploit of Luxor’s software briefly diverted 1.4% of Bitcoin’s global computing power.

An AI-assisted exploit of Luxor’s fleet-management software briefly diverted 1.4% of Bitcoin’s global computing power, netting the attacker over $10,500 while leaving the blockchain itself untouched.

A coordinated weekend cyberattack hijacked approximately 64,000 Bitcoin mining machines, temporarily redirecting up to 13 exahashes per second (EH/s) of computing power to an unauthorized address on the OCEAN mining pool.

While the incident exposed a major vulnerability in third-party mining management tools, the Bitcoin protocol itself was never compromised, and the diverted hashrate fell far short of the threshold needed to disrupt the blockchain.

Bitcoin mining hosting provider CoreX Hosting was the first to flag the suspicious activity on November 14, warning on X that thousands of machines were suddenly connecting to the OCEAN mining pool under a single external payout address.

It has been revealed that just a heads up, there is a major miner hack going on as we speak. Miners are being pointed at @ocean_mining with BTC address bc1qphukp9rjfc4rcej7erpm9ae20xmtspw8pcddrr .

Recent findings suggest that less than an hour later, approximately 13 EH/s of computing power, equivalent to about 1.4% of the entire Bitcoin network’s global hashrate, was pointing toward the attacker’s wallet. CoreX said it was working to restore the affected machines’ original mining configurations.

In a recent development, by 1:40 a.m. ET on November 15, CoreX confirmed the attack had been contained. The hashrate tied to the rogue address plunged from 13 EH/s down to roughly 100 petahashes per second (PH/s), signaling that nearly all compromised rigs had been recovered or disconnected.

Initially, blockchain trackers noted that the attacker had failed to mine a single block during the brief hijack window, suggesting the heist had yielded zero profit. However, because of how OCEAN’s payout model works, the attacker still managed to walk away with a modest payday.

Under OCEAN’s reward distribution rules, valid mining shares submitted during an active window remain eligible for payouts when the pool subsequently finds blocks.

On-chain tracking later confirmed that the attacker’s address received payouts totaling between 0.162 BTC (roughly $10,500) and 0.243 BTC across two to three block rewards before the eligible work window expired.

While the attacker’s haul was relatively small compared to the massive computing power hijacked, affected mining operators lost real-time revenue during the outage while continuing to pay electricity costs.

The incident took another turn on November 15, when mining services company Luxor confirmed that its Commander mining equipment management software had been exploited to redirect hashrate.

In a post on X, Luxor said its internal monitoring detected unauthorized pool reassignments affecting “just over a dozen” client accounts. Engineers patched the vulnerability within two hours and began reverting customer rigs to their original pools. Luxor emphasized that no user data was leaked and that its core mining pool and LuxOS firmware remained unaffected.

Last night our internal monitoring alerted us to an unauthorized redirect of hashrate through Commander. Our on-call engineering team jumped on it right away.Impact: just over a dozen client accounts. Affected machines were pointed to a different pool for a limited window. No….

In a follow-up statement, Luxor CEO Nick Hansen apologized to affected clients and said the attack involved a “sophisticated AI-enabled vector.”.

He warned that AI-powered cyberattacks are becoming an increasing threat to crypto infrastructure, with automated systems probing for vulnerabilities around the clock.

Luxor promised to fully reimburse affected clients for lost mining revenue, paying them as if their machines had continued mining normally.

The incident exposes a vulnerability in Bitcoin’s mining infrastructure that exists outside the blockchain itself. Still, it never posed a systemic threat to Bitcoin: controlling the network requires over 50% of global computing power.

At its peak, the hijacked hashrate accounted for just ~1.4% of the network and lasted only a few hours—nowhere near enough to alter transactions or double-spend coins.

Because no user wallets were drained and Bitcoin’s consensus rules operated normally, the breach had no direct impact on Bitcoin’s market price, which hovered near the $64,500–$65,000 range amid broader macro-driven market volatility.

It has been revealed that pirelli’s P Zero Trofeo RS is one of its most extreme performance tires, one capable of helping performance cars extract the most out of their potential. And that’s especially true when the organization works with automakers directly—as the Italian rubbermaker did with BMW, developed a bespoke version specifically for the BMW M range. The fresh semi-slick tire remains street legal, but doesn’t sacrifice at-the-limit grip. And it helped BMW set two new ‘Ring lap records with its BMW M2 with the M Performance Track Kit and BMW M3 CS Touring.

Industry observers note that the BMW M2 with the M Performance Track Kit managed a lap time of 7:25.068minutes. This lowered the Nürburgring Nordschleife compact car record, previously held by the M2 CS, by 0.5 seconds. The long-roof BMW M3, however, made more significant history: BMW’s M3 CS Touring lapped the 12.9-mile racetrack in 7:29.49 minutes, setting a upcoming record for the fastest touring car ever by shaving off more than five seconds. The previous touring car lap record of 7:35.06 was held by the standard BMW M3 Touring. A combination of increased horsepower, stronger brakes, and custom rubber—as well as BMW M Development engineer Jörg Weidinger behind the wheel—pushed the wagon to success.

“The bespoke development program is the result of close collaboration between Pirelli and BMW M’s R&D teams. Thanks to advanced virtual development techniques, the two teams were able to adapt the tire’s characteristics to the different requirements from the earliest stages of the project, in line with Pirelli’s Perfect Fit approach, which aims to create products tailored to each specific model or application,” the tire maker said in a statement.

Industry observers note that pirelli initially tested the tires alongside BMW at the Nürburgring Nordschleife, and the tires were also later tested at the Nardò test circuit in Italy. BMW and Pirelli have collaborated on over 30 bespoke tire projects across the P Zero family over the years, and like many others, a keen eye can tell which ones are made for Bimmers; the manufacturer-specific tires feature a BMW star marking, as a nod to the integrated development process.

David Schwartz, XRP Ledger co-architect and Ripple’s CTO Emeritus, replied to criticism of his sales with a short reminder:.

Canadian securities regulators, including the Alberta Securities Commission, British Columbia Securities Commission and Autorité des marchés financiers, are also participating.

Private-sector companies will contribute technical expertise and intelligence to help authorities identify and disrupt fraudulent networks.

It’s worth noting that the OSC didn’t provide details on how many fraud networks it is targeting, how many potential victims have been identified or how much cryptocurrency is involved in Operation Niagara.

Digital assets have changed more than the way money moves. They have also changed what users expect from digital products. A crypto holder can move between exchanges, wallets, and decentralized applications without treating every activity as a completely separate financial relationship. That expectation is increasingly influencing online gaming.

Recent findings suggest that for many players, the traditional model of maintaining one account for sports betting, another for slots, and a third for live casino games feels unnecessarily fragmented. A unified platform offers a simpler alternative: one account, one balance, and a consistent payment experience across several forms of entertainment.

Sources indicate that the appeal is particularly relevant to crypto-aware audiences in Canada. These people are already familiar with digital wallets, network confirmations, and assets that can move across borders and applications. When they enter an online gaming environment, they often expect the same degree of continuity.

Industry observers note that the strongest argument for a unified platform is practical rather than promotional. Separate gaming accounts create separate balances, deposit histories, and withdrawal processes. Players may need to move funds repeatedly, learn different interfaces, and review different sets of account information.

A shared account reduces those steps. Funds deposited for a weekend sporting event may remain available for a slot session or a live-dealer table without requiring another external transfer. The player still decides how and when the balance is used, but the platform does not force a new payment journey for every product category.

This model can be especially useful when crypto is involved. Blockchain transfers are not the same as moving credits between sections of a website. Every external transaction may involve a network selection, a destination address, a fee, and a confirmation period. Keeping more activity within one verified account can reduce the number of blockchain transactions a player needs to initiate.

Recent findings suggest that A large game or market catalogue has value, but variety alone does not create a coherent experience. A genuinely unified platform also needs consistent navigation, account controls and transaction information.

It has been revealed that players should be able to identify their available balance, review deposits and withdrawals, and reach account settings without relearning the interface each time they move from sportsbook to casino. Mobile behaviour matters as well. A platform that works smoothly on desktop but becomes difficult to navigate on a phone does not deliver a truly unified experience.

The same principle applies to support and identity checks. A single account can allow the platform to maintain one verified customer profile instead of asking the user to repeat the same process for each product. It can also provide one place for limits, security settings and support history.

Industry observers note that the growth of combined platforms does not mean that sports betting, slots and live casino are becoming identical. Each product has a different rhythm.

Sports betting is event-driven. Activity often rises around major matches, tournaments and seasonal calendars. Slots and live casino games are generally available continuously. A unified platform allows those patterns to coexist without forcing players to maintain separate accounts.

That flexibility can also make the account more useful between major sporting events. A player who primarily follows football, hockey, or basketball may still prefer access to other entertainment from the same balance. Conversely, a casino-focused user may value the option to follow a major match without opening a new account elsewhere.

The commercial trend is therefore less about persuading every player to use every product and more about removing barriers when interests overlap.

According to recent reports, crypto payments can support a unified experience, but the presence of a digital asset logo does not guarantee a good payment journey. Players still need clear information about supported assets and networks, minimum amounts, processing steps, and withdrawal requirements.

Recent findings suggest that network compatibility is particularly important. The same asset may exist on several blockchains, and sending it through an unsupported network can lead to a failed or difficult recovery process. A well-designed deposit page should make the correct network and address clear before funds are sent.

Transaction visibility also matters. Blockchain explorers can show whether a transfer has been broadcast and confirmed, while the gaming account should show when the deposit has been credited. These are related but distinct stages. Clear status information reduces uncertainty.

Industry observers note that betplay illustrates the unified-platform model by bringing sportsbook, slots, and live casino products under one brand and account experience. Its relevance to a crypto publication comes from that combination: the payment layer is connected to several entertainment categories rather than a single-purpose casino product.

The practical value is continuity. A player can explore different parts of the platform without creating a upcoming account or starting a separate balance for every vertical. The brand therefore fits a broader shift in digital entertainment toward consolidated accounts and fewer payment handoffs.

According to recent reports, that does not remove the need for normal due diligence. Players should review the assets and networks at the moment supported, transaction instructions, terms, account limits, and withdrawal requirements before depositing. Product availability can also vary by location.

Any discussion of online gaming in Canada requires a regulatory qualification. Gambling is regulated at the provincial level, and the framework is not identical across the country. Ontario introduced a competitive regulated internet gaming market in April 2022, overseen by the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario and iGaming Ontario. Other provinces use different models and rules.

In a recent development, as a result, Canadian users should confirm that a platform is available where they live and that its use complies with applicable provincial requirements. They should also meet the legal gambling age in their province.

Unified crypto gaming platforms reflect a wider digital trend. Users increasingly expect one identity, one payment layer and a consistent interface across related services. In online gaming, that can mean moving between sportsbook, slots and live casino without repeating the same financial and account-management steps.

The model is not valuable simply because it places several products on one website. Its real value comes from reducing friction while keeping balances, transaction information and account controls understandable.

For crypto-aware audiences, that combination is likely to remain compelling: choice across products, continuity across sessions and fewer unnecessary transfers between platforms.
