  • Well, movement, it seems, has played an integral part.
  • But she’s also committed to consistent, everyday movement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this year, Susan Young Browne from Delaware celebrated her 108th birthday—the news of which travelled across the world. Everyone wanted to know the retired teacher’s longevity secrets. How did Susan, who had just renewed her driving license until 2033, retain such a good quality of life?

Well, movement, it seems, has played an integral part. Firstly, Susan, who still walks unassisted, told TODAY that she continues to attend chair dancing classes at a local community centre.

But she’s also committed to consistent, everyday movement.

Susan begins every morning with a 10-minute stretching, strengthening, and balancing routine.

With flexibility, mobility, strength and balance all being key markers of longevity, Susan’s routine is a reminder that workouts do not need to be long and complicated to have far-reaching benefits.

Another key part of Susan’s daily exercise routine that likely contributes to her impressive healthspan (the number of years spent living in good health and free from chronic disease)? Her focus on leg strength.

“I get up and stand against the wall and exercise my legs. I make sure my legs are exercised,” Susan told TODAY.

Not only do strong legs help us move freely and reduce fall risk, but a growing body of evidence also points to an association between lower-body strength and cognitive function—another key element of longevity.

One oft-cited study found that older adults with greater leg strength had 34% lower odds of low cognitive function than those with weaker legs. Meanwhile, a 10-year study of more than 300 twin sisters reported “a striking protective relationship” between leg power and cognition. The twin with greater leg power at the beginning of the study maintained their cognitive function better and demonstrated fewer age-related brain changes over the following decade.

While the exact mechanisms behind this association remain unclear, among scientists’ hypotheses are that stronger muscles may improve blood flow to the brain, that resistance training may influence nervous system function, and that lower-body strength can help preserve walking speed and mobility—both of which have been associated with a lower risk of dementia.

Using a wall for support, Susan can be seen balancing on one leg, which is a simple, effective, single-leg exercise that supports strength and balance.

In a recent development, another simple move that only requires a wall? As the name suggests, a wall sit.

“Defined as an isometric exercise—an exercise where the working muscle doesn’t change length during the exercise and the joint doesn’t move—wall sits are super safe to perform, and put very little stress on the spine,” personal trainer Aimee Victoria Long previously explained to Women’s Health.

Mainly targeting the quadriceps (the muscles at the front of your thigh that support knee stability and everyday functional movements such as walking, getting up from a chair, and climbing stairs), wall sits can also improve endurance, balance, core, and lower-back strength.

Industry observers note that another simple, no-equipment exercise that supports functional lower-body strength is the humble bodyweight squat. Plus, one study even found that doing 60 seconds of squatting exercises during long periods of sitting may help preserve cognitive function.

An NCTJ-accredited journalist, Hannah graduated from Loughborough University with a BA in English and Sport Science and an MA in Media and Cultural Analysis. She has been covering sports, health and fitness for the last five years and has created content for outlets including BBC Sport, BBC Sounds, Runner’s World and Stylist. She especially enjoys interviewing those working within the community to improve access to sport, exercise and wellness. Hannah is a 2024 John Schofield Trust Fellow and was also named a 2022 Rising Star in Journalism by The Printing Charity. A keen runner, Hannah was firmly a sprinter growing up (also dabbling in long jump) but has since transitioned to longer-distance running. While 10K is her favoured race distance, she loves running or volunteering at parkrun every Saturday, followed, of course, by pastries. She’s always looking for fun latest runs and races to do and brunch spots to try.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Range Rover is pulling the plug on its two most affordable models, the Evoque and Velar, as a latest entry-level EV steps in.

For decades, the Range Rover name was viewed as a status symbol, mostly used by wealthy buyers, high-powered executives, and even royalty.

That started to change with the launch of the Evoque in 2011 and the Velar in 2017, making the iconic British luxury brand a little more accessible.

In a recent development, in the US, the 2026 Range Rover Evoque starts at $49,900, and the Velar starts at $61,600. That’s considerably less than the Sport and flagship Range Rover SUVs, which start at $83,700 and $107,400, respectively.

Industry observers note that range Rover’s accessible luxury era is reportedly drawing to a close. Martin Limbert, Range Rover’s managing director, confirmed to Autocar that the Evoque and Velar will officially be discontinued, with production set to end in 2027.

While it has no direct replacement planned, the new Range Rover GT will serve as the brand’s new entry-level vehicle.

It has been revealed that range Rover revealed the GT in July, presenting it as the fifth and newest member of the lineup. Unlike the distinct SUV design Range Rover has built the brand on, the GT is a low-slung grand tourer.

The electric GT is “a captivating new expression” of the brand, Range remarked, describing it as “the most technologically sophisticated” model it’s ever designed.

According to recent reports, it’s expected to be among the first vehicles based on JLR’s fresh EMA platform. Initially, the Range Rover GT will launch as a battery-electric vehicle (BEV), but Range Rover intends to add a full-hybrid (HEV) option later in the lifecycle.

Production of the Range Rover GT is set to begin in the first half of 2027 at JLR’s Halewood, UK plant, following the flagship electric SUV and smaller Sport EV model (shown below).

It has been revealed that the Range Rover GT is expected to start at around $90,000 with an EPA range of at least 300 miles when it goes on sale as a 2028 model. In the UK, it will likely be over £75,000 ($100,000).

Range Rover’s flagship electric SUV starts at $140,450 in the US, and the smaller Sport EV will likely be a bit cheaper at around $120,000 to $130,000.

At $90,000, the electric GT isn’t what most would consider an “entry-level” vehicle, but it’s part of Range Rover’s push into higher-end, more profitable models.

#5716. Sweden’s H100 Taps Coinbase Prime and Deribit for Its 3,506 Bitcoin Treasury as It Courts Family Offices

Sweden’s H100 Taps Coinbase Prime and Deribit for Its 3,506 Bitcoin Treasury as It Courts Family Offices

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Swedish bitcoin treasury firm H100 Group mentioned Monday it will use Coinbase Prime and the Deribit derivatives exchange for custody, trading and financing of its roughly 3,506 BTC, a move it notes supports both its bitcoin-per-share goal and a push to serve wealthy investors.
  • H100, which trades on Stockholm’s NGM Nordic SME under the ticker H100, announced the partnership in a release Monday morning.
  • H100 valued its holdings at about SEK 2.3 billion, or $226 million, based on a bitcoin price of $64,600 on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Swedish bitcoin treasury firm H100 Group mentioned Monday it will use Coinbase Prime and the Deribit derivatives exchange for custody, trading and financing of its roughly 3,506 BTC, a move it notes supports both its bitcoin-per-share goal and a push to serve wealthy investors.

H100, which trades on Stockholm’s NGM Nordic SME under the ticker H100, announced the partnership in a release Monday morning. The organization and its subsidiaries will use Coinbase and Deribit, which Coinbase owns, for custody, trading and financing, it said.

H100 valued its holdings at about SEK 2.3 billion, or $226 million, based on a bitcoin price of $64,600 on Nov. 15. It also has about SEK 219 million ($22 million) in outstanding convertible loans that carry 0% interest, mature on July 9, 2030, and equal less than 10% of the stated value of its bitcoin.

The release did not disclose fees, collateral terms or borrowing limits. It also didn’t say whether H100 has drawn on any financing, how much of its bitcoin will sit with Coinbase, or whether it is moving coins from another custodian.

H100 described Coinbase’s offering as the crypto version of a bank’s prime brokerage desk, bringing custody, financing and trade execution under one roof.

It has been revealed that the trading itself will be run in-house. PDI AS, a wholly owned trading and technology unit, builds the software and trading systems used to manage H100’s bitcoin, and the tech giant remarked those tools operate “with protecting H100’s Bitcoin holdings as the first priority.”.

“This partnership gives H100 stronger tools for our own balance sheet, and we use them on our own Bitcoin first,” Executive Chairman Sander Andersen said. “Bitcoin per share remains the measure we run the Company by, and these tools are there to help us deliver on it, not to add risk.”.

Andersen added that this is “the first of several” partnerships, “and the next is already under way.” He did not name the next partner.

Lauren Abendschein, head of institutional sales at Coinbase, said bitcoin treasury companies “have grown into an established part of our institutional client base,” and that their priorities are custody, “liquidity when the market moves, and financing against the same balance sheet.”.

Recent findings suggest that the second goal is bigger. H100 remarked it wants to become what majority shareholder Geir Harald Hansen, in a June 11 letter to shareholders, called “a leading European alternative and digital asset manager.” It will start with family offices and high-net-worth individuals looking for a partner on bitcoin investments and financing, and said it will share details as products launch.

Industry observers note that H100 began as a health-tech firm before adopting a bitcoin treasury strategy in 2025. It agreed in January to buy Swiss treasury firm Future Holdings and closed that deal in February.

According to recent reports, its holdings tripled in August. After shareholders approved the acquisition of two Norwegian holding companies in June, H100 closed the deal on Aug. 10, adding 2,455.37 BTC and lifting its total to 3,506.4 BTC, according to its second-quarter report.

Industry observers note that H100 paid for that deal with 790.5 million upcoming shares. That took its share count to about 1.13 billion and left Hansen with about 69.2% of the firm. Eirik Grøttum, who has worked with Hansen for years, became H100’s CEO the next day.

Grøttum wrote in the same report that simply raising money to buy bitcoin “is unlikely to be sufficient on its own” for treasury companies, adding that “BTC should be the hurdle rate, not the business model.”.

Sources indicate that the announcement comes as bitcoin trades near $64,000 after a weekend slide to its lowest level since July, and treasury companies face pressure to show they can grow their bitcoin per share without issuing too much stock. H100 has not noted whether it plans to buy more bitcoin.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • After announcing the name of its new midsize electric pickup this summer, Ford mentioned the Fathom will start at just $28,350 for the standard-range model.
  • According to recent reports, even with the $1,595 delivery fee, prices will start at under $30,000.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ford’s upcoming Fathom electric pickup will be among the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at $28,350. Even pricier trims will start at under $40,000.

After announcing the name of its new midsize electric pickup this summer, Ford mentioned the Fathom will start at just $28,350 for the standard-range model.

According to recent reports, even with the $1,595 delivery fee, prices will start at under $30,000. On the organization’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Jim Farley said the Fathom, Ford’s first vehicle off the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, remains on track to launch in Q4 2027.

Last Tuesday, a day before earnings, Farley said he had the chance to test-drive a prototype and that it “completely blew me away.”.

The 0 to 60 mph, huge room inside, and the hands-free, ADAS experience was like “something I’ve never experienced,” Farley told investors.

Ford’s CEO added that the Fathom is a “breakthrough product” that’s highly capable and affordable. The MSRP under $30,000 and low cost of ownership, Farley mentioned, is perfect for today’s market.

Industry observers note that the electric pickup will use a zonal electrical architecture and a 48-volt system to cut costs. It will also offer bidirectional charging, enabling it to power your home to save on energy costs or during an outage.

When asked how the company plans to upsell the Fathom beyond the $28,350 starting price, Andrew Frick, president of Ford Model e, offered some insight.

“The starting price of $28,350 is just that,” Frick noted. “We’ll have a range that goes to the high $30,000 range. And we’ll have a couple of different offerings within that,” he explained.

Frick noted it’s too soon to share more about the offerings themselves at this point, and more details will come closer to launch.

According to Farley, the embedded Apple Maps is a “game changer” for any EV, but especially for a vehicle starting under $30,000.

“That is going to be the most exciting upsell opportunity,” Farley said, “it’s really the long-term subscription and digital experience for the customer.”.

Apple Maps will be directly integrated into the navigation system. All Fathom models will be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving with standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

We still haven’t seen the interior, but Ford claims the Fathom has a “large touchscreen display” with easy-to-use navigation.

According to recent reports, I almost feel like the Fathom will be utilized similarly to how the Maverick is utilized and possibly become a big seller as well. It seems well suited for a small business work vehicle as well with fuel savings by going electric to add to the appeal.

The midsize electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, and that’s not including the frunk (front trunk) or truck bed. Ford also noted the Fathom will cost less to own over five years than a three-year-old used Tesla Model Y.

We also know the Fathom will have an NACS port after a prototype was caught at a Tesla Supercharger a few months ago.

Ford is set to open preorders in early 2027, with an official launch expected in the fourth quarter of 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • General Motors (GM) issued a recall affecting more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs because a software glitch can cause a temporary loss of braking.
  • It has been revealed that the recall comes after a 2024 Cadillac Lyriq ran into a garage (at a low speed).
  • After internal testing, GM was able to replicate the glitch, similar to a recall it issued in 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

General Motors (GM) issued a recall affecting more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs because a software glitch can cause a temporary loss of braking.

It has been revealed that the recall comes after a 2024 Cadillac Lyriq ran into a garage (at a low speed). On April 10, 2026, a GM tech expert submitted a report to GM’s Speak Up for Safety (SUFS) program for review.

After internal testing, GM was able to replicate the glitch, similar to a recall it issued in 2024. GM remarked the issue stems from a software glitch with the brake system control module (BSCM) that can cause a temporary loss of braking while driving under certain conditions.

When drivers lightly tap the brakes during a sharp turn and the vehicle hits a bump, the software’s slip calculation may misinterpret wheel movement.

In some instances, it can lead to a temporary loss of braking. The glitch only affects pAWD vehicles, including certain Cadillac Lyriq, Celestiq, Vistiq, and Chevy Blazer EV.

In a letter sent to the NHTSA on October 29, GM said the recall impacted 67,380 vehicles total, including certain:.

Industry observers note that according to documents filed with the NHTSA, GM found 24 field complaints related to the issue. Of these, 20 involved minor accidents, and two involved allegations of minor injuries.

The complaints were received between February 24, 2024, and June 11, 2026. GM mentioned it has implemented software corrections in production over the past few months.

GM will enhancement the BSCM software via an over-the-air (OTA) update or through a dealer, free of charge.

Recent findings suggest that owner notification letters are expected to be mailed out on December 14, 2026. In the meantime, you can contact Cadillac’s customer service at 1-800-333-4223 or Chevrolet’s customer service at 1-800-222-1020. GM’s recall number is N262570900.

You can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the nhtsa.gov website for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V717.

Hong Kong to License Crypto Dealers and Custodians by Year-End

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hong Kong will introduce a bill before the end of the year to bring crypto dealers, advisers, asset managers and custodians under a licensing regime, Financial Secretary Paul Chan said Monday, even as the city has approved only two of 36 first-round applicants to problem stablecoins.
  • It has been revealed that chan delivered the remarks in a keynote at the Bloomberg Global Regulatory Forum in Hong Kong.
  • Sources indicate that the proposal would amend the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance, expanding a regime that now covers virtual asset trading platforms, the government told the Legislative Council on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hong Kong will introduce a bill before the end of the year to bring crypto dealers, advisers, asset managers and custodians under a licensing regime, Financial Secretary Paul Chan said Monday, even as the city has approved only two of 36 first-round applicants to problem stablecoins.

It has been revealed that chan delivered the remarks in a keynote at the Bloomberg Global Regulatory Forum in Hong Kong. “Before the end of this year, we will introduce a bill to complete the regulatory perimeter, extending licensing to those who deal in, advise on, manage and act as custodians of digital assets,” he noted.

Sources indicate that the proposal would amend the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance, expanding a regime that now covers virtual asset trading platforms, the government told the Legislative Council on Nov. 4.

“On stablecoins, we have moved forward step by step. Of the 36 applicants in the first round, two received licences in April, and both have since introduced Hong Kong dollar stablecoins,” Chan noted. He said the emphasis is on “genuine use cases and credible business models,” citing cross-border payments as an example.

The Stablecoins Ordinance took effect in August 2025. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority granted the two issuer licenses this April, the government said in that earlier Legislative Council reply. Chan did not name the two issuers or say when a further application round might open.

The low approval rate is the point. Hong Kong is trying to build a regulated digital-asset market without opening the door to every issuer that applies.

“Our principle is simple: same activity, same risks, same regulation,” Chan remarked. On tokenisation, he said funds offered to the public in Hong Kong have grown about seven-fold in a year, and that since last month two tokenised money market funds have traded around the clock on a licensed platform. “Our approach is consistent: the same requirements as for conventional products, with additional safeguards for the new risks.”.

Industry observers note that those figures line up with a fuller count the government gave on Nov. 4. As of the end of September, the Securities and Futures Commission had authorized 17 retail tokenised products, including 13 tokenised money market funds, with about HK$10.3 billion in assets in their tokenised classes. Two of those money market funds began round-the-clock secondary trading on licensed platforms on Oct. 26.

“Above all, we are firm on one point: Decentralisation does not mean less accountability,” Chan mentioned.

It has been revealed that hong Kong already licenses virtual asset trading platforms. The upcoming bill is meant to pull dealing, advisory, management and custody work into the same ordinance, a step the government has framed as streamlining the legal perimeter rather than writing a new one from scratch.

Acting Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Joseph Chan told lawmakers on Nov. 4 that international platforms may apply for a license if they meet the statutory tests and the securities regulator’s rules, and that the coming bill is intended to let a wider range of service providers operate in the city. The government did not give a date for when the bill would be introduced, beyond “by the end of this year,” and did not say how long lawmakers would have to debate it.

Hong Kong has spent recent years trying to position itself as a regional hub for digital assets, even as other Asian financial centers have rolled out their own licensing regimes. Chan’s speech did not mention bitcoin by name, but the firms that deal in, advise on, manage and hold bitcoin in the city would fall under the expanded perimeter once the bill becomes law.

If the bill reaches the Legislative Council before year-end, dealers and custodians that have so far sat outside the platform-licensing regime will have to decide whether to apply, or to stay out of Hong Kong.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the first time, electric equipment assets are being put to work in the National Wildlife Refuge System, where a battery-powered, zero-emission ECR25 Electric compact excavator and L25 Electric compact wheel loader made by Volvo CE are making the wild more accessible to everyone.

Construction work isn’t exactly welcome in the wilderness – between diesel exhaust, engine noises, and the constant rumble of heavy machinery, even a relatively small project can have a significant impact on the native wildlife. To minimize that impact, US Fish and Wildlife Service is turning to Volvo CE and its compact excavators and wheel loaders to get the job done, building out a fresh, ADA accessible trail in Virginia’s Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge.

“We are excited to partner with the US Fish and Wildlife Service on this project to demonstrate Volvo’s commitment to lowering emissions and working to build the future we all want and need,” mentioned Dr. Ray Gallant, VP of Product Management and Productivity, Volvo CE. “Projects like the one at the Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge give a glimpse of how electric machines can create a more climate-friendly future for the construction industry.”.

Sources indicate that the refuge is home to a diverse array of grasslands, wetlands, and woods that attract red foxes, painted turtles, osprey, river otters, and countless other rarely seen species – and the ADA accessible path being laid down by the L25 Electric compact wheel loader will allow wheelchair-bound visitors to travel a half-mile-long trail around one of the pond. Meanwhile, the ECR25 Electric compact excavator will be digging trenches to improve drainage from the pond and helping to place a viewing platform that extends out over the water.

Keeping the machines running is a portable EV ARC solar-powered charging system from Beam Global that’s designed to drive down the project’s carbon footprint even further.

The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday denied Custodia Bank’s petition to review the Federal Reserve’s refusal to give the Wyoming bitcoin bank a master account, ending chief executive Caitlin Long’s years-long fight for direct access to the central bank’s payment rails.

The case, Custodia Bank, Inc. v. Federal Reserve Board of Governors, No. 26-62, is listed under “certiorari denied” on the Court’s Monday order list. The denial leaves in place a Tenth Circuit ruling that regional Federal Reserve Banks have discretion to reject even eligible applicants, and it closes the last court path Custodia had to force the Fed’s hand.

A master account is a bank’s account at a Federal Reserve Bank, and the entry point to Fedwire and other payment services. Without one, a state-chartered bank has to rely on a correspondent institution to move money.

Custodia is a Wyoming special purpose depository institution, a charter that bars it from making loans and requires dollar deposits to be fully reserved in liquid assets. After receiving that charter, it applied for a master account at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City in October 2020. In January 2021, the Kansas City Fed confirmed the bank was legally eligible and told it there were “no showstoppers.” In August 2021, Custodia also applied for Federal Reserve membership.

While those requests sat pending, the Board of Governors in August 2022 published guidelines for evaluating master-account applications. The rules put firms that are neither federally insured nor supervised by a federal banking agency into “Tier 3,” the group that “generally receive[s] the strictest level of review.” Custodia fell into that bucket.

On January 27, 2023, the Kansas City Fed denied the master account, citing an “unprecedented” business model “narrowly focused on crypto-asset activities” and concluding the risks were “highly likely” to be “inconsistent with safe and sound banking practices.” The same day, the Board denied Custodia’s membership application, saying approval “would be inconsistent with the financial, managerial, and corporate powers factors.”.

It has been revealed that custodia had already sued the Fed and the Kansas City Fed in June 2022 over the delay. On March 29, 2024, U.S. District Judge Scott W. Skavdahl in Wyoming ruled that the Federal Reserve Act gives Reserve Banks discretion to grant or deny master accounts, dismissed Custodia’s Administrative Procedure Act claim for lack of a final agency action, and granted the Kansas City Fed summary judgment.

In a recent development, the Tenth Circuit affirmed on October 31, 2025, in a 2-1 decision Bitcoin Magazine covered at the time. Judge David Ebel, joined by Judge Veronica Rossman, held that Section 342 of the Federal Reserve Act, which indicates a Reserve Bank “may receive” deposits, is discretionary, and that the Monetary Control Act of 1980’s instruction that Fed services “shall be available” to nonmember banks is a pricing rule, not a right to an account.

It has been revealed that tymkovich dissented. “We are bound by the ordinary language of the statute and, in my view, shall means shall,” he wrote. The 1980 law, he said, “mandates access to the Fed’s payment services for all nonmember depository institutions.” On March 13, 2026, the full Tenth Circuit denied rehearing, with Judges Hartz, Tymkovich and Eid voting to grant. Being denied a master account, Tymkovich wrote in that later dissent, is “akin to a death sentence.”.

Custodia’s July petition, filed by Kannon Shanmugam, asked whether the Monetary Control Act “gives presidents of regional Federal Reserve Banks discretionary authority to deny master accounts” to legally eligible nonmember banks. The Board and the Kansas City Fed opposed review. The Court distributed the case for its Nov. 13 conference and turned it down today.

Sources indicate that the practical effect is that a state charter, even one that makes a bank legally eligible, does not guarantee a door into the Fed’s payment system. Crypto-focused banks and other novel charters now have little judicial recourse, at least in the Tenth Circuit, if a Reserve Bank turns them away. Critics have long described that pattern of exclusion, and of banks cutting off crypto firms, as Operation Choke Point 2.0.

Neither Custodia nor Long had commented on the Supreme Court’s denial as of 10:07 a.m. ET Monday.

Industry News: Harvard Holds 3.04 Million Bitcoin ETF Shares Steady

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (624 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Harvard Management Organization left its stake in BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust unchanged at 3,044,612 shares in the third quarter, a position valued at $144.1 million as of Sept.
  • According to recent reports, the university’s endowment manager disclosed the holding in a Form 13F filed Friday, covering the quarter ended Sept.
  • Industry observers note that the same 3,044,612 shares were worth $101.4 million on June 30 and $117.0 million on March 31, so the position rose in value during the third quarter as bitcoin recovered, then gave back a large share of that gain after the quarter ended.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Harvard Management Organization left its stake in BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust unchanged at 3,044,612 shares in the third quarter, a position valued at $144.1 million as of Sept. 30 and now worth about $110.6 million after bitcoin’s slide.

According to recent reports, the university’s endowment manager disclosed the holding in a Form 13F filed Friday, covering the quarter ended Sept. 30. The share count is the same one Harvard reported on June 30 and on March 31. At 10:40 a.m. ET Monday, IBIT traded at $36.32, putting the stake at about $110.6 million, a paper decline of roughly $33.6 million, or 23%, from the value in the filing. The Sept. 30 close of $47.34 matches the price implied by the reported value.

Industry observers note that the same 3,044,612 shares were worth $101.4 million on June 30 and $117.0 million on March 31, so the position rose in value during the third quarter as bitcoin recovered, then gave back a large share of that gain after the quarter ended. Even after the November slide, the stake is still worth more than it was at midyear.

IBIT was Harvard’s eighth-largest position among 18 holdings in a 13F portfolio valued at $3.95 billion, or about 3.6% of that publicly disclosed book of U.S. securities, which does not include the rest of the endowment. The largest holding was Space Exploration Technologies, reported at $1.29 billion. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing was second, at $616.5 million. That ranking is a sharp change from late 2025, when the bitcoin ETF was Harvard’s largest publicly disclosed position.

Recent findings suggest that harvard first reported an IBIT position in its filing for the quarter ended June 30, 2025: 1,906,000 shares worth $116.7 million. It had not listed the fund in earlier 13Fs, including the report for March 31, 2025. By Sept. 30, 2025, Harvard had tripled the stake to 6,813,612 shares, valued at $442.9 million, making IBIT its largest public holding.

According to recent reports, the endowment trimmed that position by about 21% in the fourth quarter of 2025, to 5,353,612 shares worth $265.8 million, and opened a first stake in BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust of 3,870,900 shares, valued at $86.8 million. It cut the bitcoin ETF again in the first quarter of 2026, by about 2.31 million shares, or 43%, to the 3,044,612 shares it still reported on Sept. 30, and sold the Ethereum fund entirely. The latest filing lists no other bitcoin or crypto ETFs. The remaining IBIT position is still larger, in share terms, than the 1.91 million shares Harvard first disclosed.

Industry observers note that harvard’s gold ETFs are now much larger than its bitcoin position. The same 13F lists 1,161,000 shares of SPDR Gold Shares worth $442.2 million, the portfolio’s third-largest holding, and 1,980,085 shares of the iShares Gold Trust worth $154.6 million. Combined, the two gold funds were valued at $596.8 million, more than four times the IBIT stake. The iShares Gold Trust share count was unchanged from June 30. The SPDR Gold Shares position jumped from 58,862 shares at midyear.

Bitcoin traded near $64,200 as of 10:40 a.m. ET Monday, down about 17% in November from an Oct. 31 close near $77,400, and down about 23% from about $83,550 at the end of September. Since the quarter closed, U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs have been seeing heavy redemptions. IBIT bled about $2 billion over nine straight sessions through mid-November, and the funds as a group extended their outflow streak to seven sessions through Friday, losing about $1.91 billion since Nov. 5.

It has been revealed that the 13F is a snapshot of holdings as of Sept. 30. It does not show whether Harvard bought or sold any IBIT shares in October or November.

What Is Canton Network? The Privacy Blockchain Built for Wall Street

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The majority of blockchains are designed in such a way that anyone can see every transaction, every balance and every smart contract call.
  • While that may work for retail crypto traders, banks, asset managers and clearinghouses can't work that way.
  • Industry observers note that canton Network was built to fix that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The majority of blockchains are designed in such a way that anyone can see every transaction, every balance and every smart contract call.

While that may work for retail crypto traders, banks, asset managers and clearinghouses can't work that way. They can't show their trading positions, client data or collateral flows to competitors, and privacy and confidentiality rules require them to protect client information.

Industry observers note that canton Network was built to fix that. It is a public layer-1 blockchain designed for privacy-preserving transactions, in which data is shared only with the parties involved. Institutions can concern, trade and settle tokenized assets such as Treasuries, stocks, funds and stablecoins together on one shared network, and each party only sees the data it is entitled to see.

According to recent reports, canton began as a niche enterprise project from software firm Digital Asset. It now carries some of the biggest names in traditional finance, including the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), the post-trade backbone of U.S. markets, which introduced its tokenization service on Canton and its own private network in October 2026.

This guide covers what Canton is, how its privacy model works, who is building on it and what its native token, Canton Coin (CC), does.

Recent findings suggest that canton Network is a layer-1 blockchain developed by Digital Asset, a Newly introduced York organization founded in 2014 that has long built distributed ledger software for financial firms. Canton introduced in May 2023 with a pilot group that included Goldman Sachs, Deloitte, Microsoft and others. Its public infrastructure, the Global Synchronizer, went live in July 2024 together with Canton Coin.

Sources indicate that canton is better described as a "network of networks" than as one massive ledger. Each institution runs its own validator node and applications, and its node stores only the data relevant to it, according to Canton's documentation. The nodes connect through the Global Synchronizer, so assets and transactions can move between them atomically: a trade either settles fully on every side or not at all.

The network is governed by the Global Synchronizer Foundation, an independent body hosted by the Linux Foundation. A group of "Super Validators" operates the Global Synchronizer.

Sources indicate that in June 2026, Digital Asset raised $355 million in a round led by a16z crypto. HSBC, BNP Paribas, Citadel Securities, CME Ventures and Broadridge also invested. That followed a $135 million round in June 2025.

Canton's key idea is sub-transaction privacy. Smart contracts on Canton are written in Daml, Digital Asset's open-source contract language. Daml spells out exactly which parties are signatories and observers on each contract. When a transaction runs, each participant's node receives only the parts it is involved in.

It has been revealed that think of a repo trade between two banks with a custodian in the middle. Each party sees and checks its own leg. Nobody else on the network sees the details, and the synchronizer orders and confirms the transaction without reading its contents.

This is very different from Ethereum-style chains, where every node replicates every state change. On Canton, the Global Synchronizer, run by the Super Validators, orders encrypted messages and confirms transactions without seeing their contents, while each institution's own validator node holds its data. Institutions keep control of their data, but can avoid much of the reconciliation that legacy systems require. In practice, most activity on the network is private: about 79% of the updates recorded on Canton in a 24-hour period in November 2026 were private, according to CantonScan.

"Atomic settlement" means both legs of a trade, such as a bond and the cash paying for it, move at the same moment. That removes the risk that one side delivers and the other doesn't.

What sets Canton apart is who uses it. Recent milestones include:.

Canton Coin (CC) is the native utility token of the Global Synchronizer. Users pay network fees by burning CC. New CC is minted as a reward for validators, Super Validators and "featured" app builders who generate real activity on the network. This setup is called a burn-mint equilibrium.

Recent findings suggest that CC had no pre-mine and no allocations to venture capital investors, according to Canton: every token in circulation has been earned through minting rewards, which are split between Super Validators, app builders and validators. Whether supply shrinks depends on usage. As of November 2026, the network was burning roughly 80% as much CC each day as it minted, according to CantonScan data, below the 1:1 ratio at which supply would start to shrink. Circulating supply stood at just over 40 billion CC.

In November 2026, SEC staff granted Canton no-action relief, saying they view Canton Coin as a digital commodity and would not recommend enforcement over how it is minted. In May 2026, 21Shares launched the first U.S. ETF offering direct exposure to CC.

Institutional custody is catching up. Ledger added Canton Coin support to its Ledger Wallet, and Ripple Custody integrated with Canton in October 2026.

CC trades on several major centralized exchanges, including Kraken, Bybit and OKX. CC perpetual futures are also available on Binance Futures, and Alchemy Pay supports buying CC with a card. On Canton itself, Cantex offers onchain swaps. CC is a native coin, not an ERC-20 token, so be wary of look-alike "CC" tokens on Ethereum-based DEXs. You can track Canton Coin's latest price on Decrypt's price page.

Availability varies by region, and nothing in this guide is investment advice.

Canton's next phase is moving from pilots to full production. DTCC's service is now live, and its roadmap adds onchain settlement, collateral management and digital cash. Derivnex and its partners plan to bring cash settlement and collateral management for derivatives directly onto Canton. Expansion in Asia is also picking up: Shinhan Financial Group, Hanwha Investment & Securities, LG CNS and Meritz Securities have all signed Canton deals.

It has been revealed that canton doesn't have a monopoly, though. DTCC intends to connect its tokenization service to Stellar, Circle's Arc and Solana in 2027.

For CC holders, the significant question is whether institutional activity grows fast enough that burns outpace issuance. Canton is betting that Wall Street wants privacy and interoperability on a public network, and it has signed up an unusually long list of major financial institutions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices are driving an unprecedented number of used car buyers to consider going electric, and that increased demand without a corresponding increase in supply means these used EVs are flying off dealer lots.

Sources indicate that days on the lot. That’s dealer-speak for the average number of days a given vehicle typically sits in inventory before finding a buyer. That’s critically important to dealers, since the vehicles on their lots are commonly financed through something called floorplan credit, and every additional day a car spends on a dealer’s lot can mean another day of interest payments and another day closer to a curtailment. Days on the lot can be even more important to dealers when it comes to cars owned outright, as well, as the dealers can have significant cash tied up in vehicles they’ve purchased outright, and every day those cars sit is another day that money isn’t working for them elsewhere.

That’s what makes this month’s fastest-selling used EVs particularly interesting, because these used EVs aren’t just selling fast for electric vehicles – they’re selling fast, period.

Dealer news sources Automotive News and Cox Automotive report that the average latest car spent 82 days on the lot in October, with a 75-day target being an industry-wide benchmark. At the same time, the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron Quattro with its 258-mile EPA-estimated range is turning in just 29.8 days. (!).

According to recent reports, that Audi’s not alone. In a recently-released vehicle pricing study, iSeeCars reported that the Toyota BZ4x, Lexus RZ300e, Honda Prologue, and Borrás-family favorite Polestar 2 are all turning in an average of 35 days or less, with the BMW i4, iX, Kia EV6, and Chevrolet Equinox EV just a day or two behind.

“The results reveal a market where EVs are appreciating in average asking price much faster than other drivetrains, while also spending less time waiting for buyers,” stated iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer, who found that average transaction prices for EVs rose 9.8% last month as ICE-powered vehicles stayed steady, rising just 0.3%. “Hybrids are experiencing moderate improvements in price and selling speed, while gasoline-powered vehicles have seen their selling times increase,” he adds, “despite relatively stable prices.”.

@Jo Borras , you forgot to mention about one more factor (besides: "A newly introduced car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices..."). Back in September last year there was still electric vehicle tax credits in the United States that has ended on September 30, 2025.

Used electric vehicles averaged a price of $32,533 in September 2026, up $2,896 from the $29,637 ATP recorded a year earlier.

BLUETTI’s flexible $1,099 Apex 200 backs up your home – and powers your RV

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What do you actually need to keep running when the power goes out?
  • The Apex 200 starts with 2.56kWh of storage and 3.2kW of continuous AC output, with the option to add batteries when you need longer backup.
  • It has been revealed that BLUETTI launches the Apex 200 on November 4, with standalone super early-bird pricing starting at $1,099 through November 18.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What do you actually need to keep running when the power goes out? For most households, the fridge, wifi, phones, and a few other essentials come first. Buying enough battery storage for every appliance in the house can come later – and that’s the appeal of BLUETTI’s latest launch, the Apex 200 portable power station.

The Apex 200 starts with 2.56kWh of storage and 3.2kW of continuous AC output, with the option to add batteries when you need longer backup. Built-in RV connections also mean it can earn its keep between blackouts.

It has been revealed that BLUETTI launches the Apex 200 on November 4, with standalone super early-bird pricing starting at $1,099 through November 18. Electrek readers can get an extra 5% off with code ELECTREK5OFF.

Here’s how to work out which setup is worth buying for your home or RV.

The Apex 200 takes the expandable design of BLUETTI’s flagship Apex series and puts it in a smaller package.

You get a 2,560Wh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery. The 3.2kW of continuous AC output increases to 3.6kW when an expansion battery is connected or the unit is actively charging.

In a recent development, the enclosure holds all that in 36.2 liters and weighs 26.9kg (59.3 lb). You’ll want two hands to move it, but it’s convenient to move it between home and your camper.

BLUETTI’s UltraCell technology delivers an industry-leading energy density of 70.7 Wh/L, yet the Apex 200 is more than 50% smaller by volume than class competitors. For an RV owner, that smaller footprint frees up room for other gear.

It has been revealed that there’s also a tilted display and four app-controllable AC outlets. That might not sound like a substantial deal, but when the battery is on the floor or under your desk and you want to check or redirect its charge, it means you don’t have to crouch.

According to recent reports, BLUETTI calls its approach “Start Small. Scale Significant. Power More.” BLUETTI says Apex 300 consumers reported liking the modular design but wanted something easier to handle day to day. The Apex 200 offers them a lower entry point, with room to add capacity rather than replace the main unit.

Before buying a portable power station, you’ll want to know how much power your appliances draw and how much energy they use over time.

In a recent development, for example, a 150W appliance running continuously for 10 hours uses 1,500Wh. A 1,500W appliance gets through that same amount in one hour. Running a coffee maker briefly is a different proposition from keeping a high-draw appliance on all afternoon.

A rough runtime calculation is: Usable battery capacity in watt-hours ÷ average load in watts = hours of operation.

Industry observers note that divide the Apex 200’s nominal 2,560Wh by a steady 150W load, and you get about 17 hours before accounting for conversion losses and the battery system’s own power use. Real runtime will be lower.

Refrigerators complicate that calculation because their compressors cycle on and off. Check measured daily energy use where possible, along with startup demand – motors can briefly draw more power when they kick on.

If your usual blackout lasts four to 12 hours, start by looking at the Apex 200 on its own.

Industry observers note that BLUETTI estimates it can run a 150W refrigerator for 10–12 hours, or support low-draw essentials such as CPAPs, wifi routers, and mobile devices for two to three days, depending on the equipment and how it’s used. That doesn’t mean every device on that list will run together for three days. Your combined load determines the runtime.

The Apex 200 also gives you more control over where that energy goes. Four independently controllable Smart AC outlets built right into the unit – no need to buy smart plugs! – let you switch individual devices on and off through the BLUETTI App, set schedules, and apply state-of-charge controls. So if something doesn’t need power overnight, you can turn off its power at the outlet and save the fridge’s battery.

Industry observers note that BLUETTI calls the feature an industry first for portable power stations. The system also works with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Home Assistant.

In a recent development, A UPS function switches connected equipment to battery power in 15 milliseconds. Check that switching time against your equipment’s requirements, especially for a CPAP or other sensitive device.

With AC output on and the display off, idle consumption drops to just 10.5W.

A winter freeze or severe storm can leave you without grid power for days. That’s when adding extra storage starts to make more sense.

For typical power outages, adding one or two BLUETTI B300K batteries can extend essential home backup to two to three days.

Sources indicate that but you can go further. One Apex 200 supports up to six B500K expansion batteries, bringing its maximum capacity to 33.28kWh.

But a bigger battery still needs recharging eventually. The Apex 200 accepts up to 3kW of solar input across two independent channels:.

With a correctly configured array of SORA 500 portable solar panels making full use of those inputs, BLUETTI says the base battery can charge from 0 to 80% in 50 minutes, or reach 100% in 1.7 hours using solar alone.

A solar generator setup lets you recharge during daylight. The Apex 200 can also be charged with wall AC, vehicle charging, and compatible gas-generator charging. A suitable 30A generator connection can help replenish the battery when solar production falls short.

The Apex 200 can also form part of a larger home battery backup system through BLUETTI’s Hub A1 parallel box.

BLUETTI specifies up to 6kW of continuous AC output and approximately 100kWh of storage across a parallel system using up to three Apex 200 units.

Sources indicate that that’s a significant increase over the standalone battery, but your daily consumption still matters. A steady 1kW load uses 24kWh in 24 hours. Heavy-draw appliances can make a large battery feel much smaller.

In a recent development, BLUETTI positions its larger configurations for three to four days of essential-panel backup. How close you get depends on your batteries, appliances, and ability to recharge.

If you want automatic backup through your home’s electrical panel, confirm the compatible transfer equipment, supported circuits, voltage, and output for the exact bundle. Those details determine what you can actually keep running.

Start with your most likely outage, then decide whether you need more runtime, a charging source, or both.

Extra batteries extend runtime. Solar panels or another charging source recharge them. For outages that stretch into days, both can be worth having.

Recent findings suggest that when shopping for a camper van or travel trailer, choosing a battery comes down to more than just capacity. Among its 10 output ports are two connections RV owners will appreciate having built in.

The native 30A TT-30R RV outlet plugs directly into travel trailer shore power inlets for 120V power.

Sources indicate that the 12V/30A Anderson port can directly power compatible DC equipment, including portable fridges and communications gear. This avoids converting battery power to AC and then back to DC, cutting out unnecessary conversion steps.

For charging between campsites, the system can pair with the BLUETTI Charger 2, which combines alternator and solar charging support. It lets you use driving time to replenish the battery through faster vehicle alternator charging, then use solar when you’re parked.

In a recent development, BLUETTI’s recommended mobile bundle is the Apex 200 + SORA 500 solar panel + Charger 2. You get storage for camp, solar charging during your stay, and alternator charging on the road. Compatible campground AC gives you another option.

Recent findings suggest that the Apex 200 is the better fit if you value a smaller enclosure, easier transport, native RV ports, and a lower upfront cost. You can start with 2.56kWh and expand to 33.28kWh on one unit, or approximately 100kWh across a fully expanded parallel system.

Industry observers note that the Apex 300 is worth considering if your priority is higher native output and capacity for a system that will mostly stay at home. It offers 3,840W of output and 2,764.8Wh of battery storage, and BLUETTI positions it for more advanced home backup, including compatible 120V/240V configurations.

In a recent development, for someone who wants a battery for both blackouts and RV trips, the Apex 200’s size and connections make a useful combination. You can buy the storage you need now and add more when your power needs change.

The Apex 200 launches November 4, with the standalone unit starting at $1,099 during the November 4–18 super early-bird promotion.

Founded in 2013, BLUETTI allows millions of people across more than 120 countries to stay safe and prepared. Its in-house R&D supports a range of solar generators and home backup systems for outage preparation, RV travel, and off-grid living and recreation.

Shop the Apex 200 and launch bundles, and use ELECTREK5OFF at checkout for an extra 5% savings.

I’ve Hiked All 7 Continents—This Is the Cold-Weather Boot I Recommend for Winter Treks

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • Industry observers note that WE’RE HALFWAY THROUGH fall (seriously?!), and that means winter is just around the corner.
  • Prepping for winter hiking is all about staying dry, warm, and comfortable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that WE’RE HALFWAY THROUGH fall (seriously?!), and that means winter is just around the corner. Colder weather and—depending on where you live and hike—snow, freezing rain, ice, and sleet are all very real possibilities on the trail in the coming months. It’s time to pack away most of your three-season hiking gear and bust out your dedicated cold-weather kit.

Prepping for winter hiking is all about staying dry, warm, and comfortable. Whether you’re looking to upgrade your current outerwear—everything from jackets and hats to hiking boots and socks—or this is your first winter hiking season, we’ve rounded up the best cold-weather hiking gear to help you tackle the trail this year. As a seasoned hiker who’s explored all seven continents over the last 30 years, this is what I recommend in 2026.

Rugged, weatherproof, and ready for the nastiest winter conditions, this newly introduced-for-2026 boot is one winter hiking boot to rule them all. But, don’t let the chunky design fool you. These are among the most comfortable, streamlined cold-weather kicks I’ve ever worn (weighing 17.5 ounces), making them versatile enough for not only winter, but challenging shoulder season hikes too.

Sources indicate that like most everything in Paka’s lineup, the Sol Crew leans on a combination of synthetic and natural fibers, giving you the best of both worlds. The Tencel-meets-alpaca construction is breathable, quick-wicking, and extremely odor-resistant. It feels great against the skin as a true base layer, and the dash of Spandex adds just the right amount of stretch. Plus, it’s versatile enough to double as a sun shirt in warmer weather with UPF 30+ sun protection.

Read More: Best Hiking Backpacks.

According to recent reports, if I had to pick just one favorite Mountain Hardwear jacket, the upcoming go-to StretchDown Jacket gets the nod. It’s warm, packable, durable, and the stretch gives it an edge over most other down jackets, with the athletic fit stretching to accommodate beefier layers in deep cold weather. That’s gotten even better with the latest update to the baffling with DoppleWeave, which catches more down and keeps it from migrating much less—making for less cold spots. Plus, it’s available in Light, Medium, and Big “weights,” so you can dial in the exact warmth level that suits your hiking style.

I’ve worn Mammut’s Runbold IV hiking pants on three continents and they’ve never let me down. This winter-ready version is just as wind-resistant and water-repellent, but the addition of a light fleece liner adds even more comfort and a just-right level of warmth. Three zippered pockets add plenty of storage options, and mesh-lined zippered vents keep you from overheating on the trail. Bonus: It’s all made with eco-friendly, bluesign-certified materials.

Recent findings suggest that keeping your feet dry at all costs is doubly key in winter when unpredictable conditions can deliver freezing rain, ice, snow, or some combination of all three. These socks are phenomenal in wet, cold weather, making them invaluable for winter hiking. They're like wearing a wetsuit bootie on your feet (except with no hinderance in range of motion).

Smartwool’s soft, natural, Merino-centric collection has been a favorite of mine for more than a decade. This OG base layer offers a more relaxed fit (compared to the suctioned-to-the-body vibe of most thermals) and a midweight warmth that’s perfect for layering under hiking pants, ski pants, or just about any cold-weather bottoms. Plus, Smartwool’s is among the softest Merino on the market.

The two-piece design adds a rolltop outer sleeve to a traditional HydraPak water bladder. The result is a setup that’s designed to keep cold water cold in the summer, but with the added benefit of keeping warm water warm for winter hikes. It also helps ensure that your water supply doesn’t straight-up freeze in deep cold conditions.

Read More: Best Hydration Packs.

I’ve been a fan of Icebreaker’s RealFleece blend for years—it’s softer and more luxurious than traditional wool but with all the benefits of natural Merino. This midweight top makes this the perfect in-between top that layers well (on top or underneath) in colder weather. The half-zip design is also great for rapidly dumping heat on the go.

In a recent development, the OG Buff is arguably the most versatile piece of apparel in my pack. This winter-ready version upgrades to Polartec fleece that’s warm, buttery soft, and fast-drying. The stretchy construction allows for wearing it any of ten different ways, and UPF 50 protection shields your neck and face on harsh sunny days.

According to recent reports, I appreciate a pair of midweight gloves that balances reliable warmth and weather resistance with enough dexterity to allow me to still use my phone, camera, and do the things that heavyweight ski gloves often make impossible on the trail. The Denali checks all of these boxes while adding a silicone grip and touchscreen-friendly fingertips to boot.

Arc’teryx’s Bird Head Toque brings a dash of understated cool to winter hiking headgear, and is amongst the most popular beanies you’ll find right now. I love the oversized classic “dinosaur bird” logo and bold color options. And the blended Merino/acrylic construction ensures that it’s soft, warm, quick-drying, and moisture-wicking—perfect for long winter days on the trail.

In a recent development, fancy rainshells can be obscenely expensive. Spyder takes most of the next-gen technical features of the best shells I’ve personally tested—four-way stretch, solid DWR, and excellent breathability—and packages them into the surprisingly affordable Clutch that’s available for under $200. Bonus: It ditches the “crinkly plastic bag” vibe of most other rain shells, keeping you quieter on the trail.

Recent findings suggest that hyperlite leans heavy on next-gen Dyneema Woven Composite 3.9 fabric, ensuring the Southwest 40 is lightweight, extremely durable, and completely weatherproof—all essential for intense winter hikes. I love the roll-top design that keeps things dead simple with just the right amount of organization and nothing more. (I also like that it’s available in 55L and 70L variations for longer expeditions.).

All modern hiking apparel is made from natural fibers, synthetic fibers, or a blend of the two. Merino and alpaca wool are my two favorite natural options, as both offer excellent thermal regulation, breathability, and odor-resistance. They’re fantastic for longer trips, allowing you to pack less and travel farther while staying dry, comfortable, and stink-free. In most cases, however, they tend to be more expensive than their synthetic counterparts.

Recent findings suggest that synthetic fibers like polyester, nylon, and polypropylene all dry faster than Merino, are typically lighter weight, and more budget-friendly. However, they don’t offer the same odor resistance, and they’re all petroleum-based products. So, they’re hardly eco-friendly.

The key is regulating your body temperature with proper layering. Start with a thin base layer that feels good against the skin and fits closely without being too restrictive. Add an insulating midlayer like a half-zip or full-zip fleece. In especially cold conditions, adding a down shirt or full down jacket will help provide extra warmth. Top it off with a final layer that’s designed for weather protection (to fend off wind and precipitation) in the form of a hard or soft shell. Gore-Tex is the gold standard for this last layer as it offers the best protection, however, it’s also the most expensive. To maintain a comfortable body temperature and ensure you don’t overheat (and sweat), shed or add layers as necessary throughout your cold weather hike. This is where having a little extra room in your pack allows for stashing those extra layers.

There are a lot of individual factors that determine which jacket is right for you, including the quality of down used and how cold or hot you tend to run personally. But fill power is often the most straightforward spec to consider when determining the warmth of a puffy or down jacket. In general, 700 to 800 fill power will keep you warm for most cold-weather hikes. Upgrade to 850-plus fill power for extreme, subzero winter conditions.

It has been revealed that it’s also important to consider the face fabric construction. Denier measures both weight and durability. For example, a 7D to 10D down jacket will be lighter and more packable, but also more prone to damage on the trail. Upgrading to a 15D-plus puffer adds weight but also durability. There’s no right answer as it depends on your budget and style of hiking.

It has been revealed that boot insulation is often measured in grams. A winter hiking boot with 200 grams of insulation should suffice in most cold weather conditions, while a 400g+ alternative is better for subzero temps, hiking in snow, or if your feet run cold. A waterproof membrane (again, Gore-Tex is best) is essential for winter boots, especially if you know you’ll be hiking in wet or snowy conditions. Finally, look for an outsole with a winter-centric tread compound with multi-directional lugs (I love Vibram Arctic Grip) for maximum traction in snow and ice.

Sources indicate that as an avid hiker and adventure travel writer for more than two decades, I've tested countless outdoor products from all of the world's most recognized brands. Whether that’s a weeklong car camping trip or backpacking throughout Utah’s national parks, I’ve assessed outdoor gear in countless different scenarios and climates. I also consulted with Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower on top options, research, and his own personal testing in the winter months.

While testing cold weather hiking gear, we've been sure to take thorough notes on comfort, warmth, ease of packing, weight, durability, functionality, performance, and necessity.

#5691. Aniioki A9 Pro Max review: Basically an electric motorcycle that you can pedal

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1403 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Aniioki A9 Pro Max review: Basically an electric motorcycle that you can pedal

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are electric bikes, there are electric motorcycles, and then there are machines like the Aniioki A9 Pro Max that plant a flag somewhere in the increasingly large no-man’s-land between the two.
  • According to recent reports, technically, it has pedals.
  • But let’s get something out of the way right at the beginning: this isn’t a street-legal electric bicycle in the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are electric bikes, there are electric motorcycles, and then there are machines like the Aniioki A9 Pro Max that plant a flag somewhere in the increasingly large no-man’s-land between the two.

According to recent reports, technically, it has pedals. You can pedal it fairly effectively too, with the actually adjustable seat. You can even pedal it for fun, which is more than I can say for some of the increasingly motorcycle-shaped “e-bikes” I’ve tested lately.

But let’s get something out of the way right at the beginning: this isn’t a street-legal electric bicycle in the US. Not when we’re talking about dual motors producing up to 6,000W of peak power and speeds of around 45 mph.

And you know what? That’s fine. As long as we’re all honest about what this thing is.

The Aniioki A9 Pro Max is absolutely massive, and the spec sheet makes that abundantly clear.

According to recent reports, the version I tested uses a pair of 2,500W direct-drive hub motors, one in each wheel, with Aniioki claiming 3,000W peak power from each motor. That gives the bike a combined peak figure of 6,000W and up to 250 Nm of combined torque. It’s hard to overstate how massive that is.

In a recent development, then there’s the battery. You can choose between a 60V 70Ah pack with 4.2 kWh of capacity or an even larger 60V 80Ah pack packing 4.8 kWh. For comparison, many typical commuter e-bikes have somewhere around 500-700 Wh of battery. The smaller battery here is roughly six to eight times that size. That’s absolutely in the territory of legit light electric motorcycles.

It has been revealed that aniioki claims up to 230+ miles (370 km) of pedal-assist range, though as usual, you should take maximum e-bike range figures as best-case numbers. Using the throttle and enjoying those big motors is going to dramatically reduce that figure. Even so, with more than 4 kWh of battery underneath you, range anxiety isn’t exactly the first thing that comes to mind.

In a recent development, all that hardware comes with a predictable penalty: weight. The 70Ah model tips the scales at around 188 lb (85 kg), while the 80Ah version approaches 193 lb (87.5 kg). Those aren’t e-bike weights. Those are motorcycle weights. Again, you can see the direction this is going.

Here’s where the A9 Pro Max gets more interesting to me.

A lot of high-powered e-motos include pedals seemingly as a regulatory fig leaf. They’re technically there, but the geometry is so bad that nobody in their right mind would want to pedal the thing farther than across a parking lot. Even some smaller and presumably Class 2 legal e-bikes that have moto-style frames are nearly unpedalable for actual riding over any reasonable distance.

But the A9 here is actually pedalable thanks to having something that more closely resembles a bicycle seat, plus adjustability that lets riders dial in the correct seat height.

The A9 Pro Max feels more like a strange combination of an oversized fat-tire e-bike and a small electric motorcycle. There’s a Shimano 7-speed drivetrain and a huge 72-tooth chainring, meaning the pedals aren’t entirely ornamental.

I actually enjoyed pedaling it with the pedal assist engaged. You’re obviously not going to mistake a nearly 200-pound machine rolling on enormous 26 x 4.8-inch tires for a lightweight fitness bike, but there’s something fun about contributing some human power while two giant hub motors do most of the heavy lifting.

And when you don’t feel like pedaling, there’s a full-twist throttle waiting for you.

Recent findings suggest that that combination is really the appeal here. You can ride it more like an e-bike when the mood strikes, or twist the throttle and treat it more like a lightweight e-moto.

Sources indicate that and again, I don’t want to beat a dead horse here, but remember: the pedals don’t make this an electric bicycle. It’s still an e-moto, but it’s one that you can actually have fun pedaling. You can treat it like a mech suit, where pedaling translates into crazy power, as if you have super-human legs. And with the insanely large 72t chainring, pedaling at higher speeds is actually doable. Though I’ll tell you right now, pedaling at 40 mph (64 km/h) is not exactly a normal or natural feeling.

And it’s worth pointing out that at a starting price of US $2,899 (or more for the larger battery capacities), that’s a fairly reasonable price compared to most e-motos that can be more limiting in how and where you can ride them.

Fortunately, Aniioki seems to understand that putting this much power on two wheels requires more serious components than the average bicycle.

The braking setup is particularly wild. There are two massive 300mm brake rotors on the front wheel and another 300mm rotor out back, along with a linked CBS braking system. The front uses custom eight-piston calipers (the pair of quad-piston calipers) while the rear gets a custom six-piston setup.

There’s also an adjustable air-suspension fork with 110mm of travel, rear suspension to smooth out bumps at higher speeds, integrated lighting and turn signals, and a large five-inch display that even incorporates features like Bluetooth audio and a recording camera.

That brings us to the elephant in the room.

Recent findings suggest that in the US, consumer-product rules generally define a low-speed electric bicycle around a motor of less than 750W and a maximum motor-powered speed below 20 mph (32 km/h), while individual states use their own operating laws that typically match the familiar Class 1/2/3 framework. A 6,000W machine capable of around 45 mph (72 km/h) blows straight through normal limits.

So please don’t see pedals and assume this belongs on your local bicycle path.

It has been revealed that where and how you can legally operate something like the A9 Pro Max depends on your local laws and whether it can qualify under another vehicle category. For many owners, the sensible place to enjoy its full performance is going to be private property or other areas where such vehicles are permitted.

According to recent reports, that caveat doesn’t make the bike itself bad. It just means buyers need to understand what they’re buying.

And judged on what it actually is rather than what the word “e-bike” on the product page suggests, I had a lot of fun on it.

There are certainly riders who would look at a nearly 200-pound, 45 mph machine and say, “Why not just buy an electric motorcycle?” That’s a perfectly reasonable question.

In addition to kW power limits, the legal boundary for what is an e-bike should also include weight. Anything over 100lbs including battery is no longer an e-bike and it carries a dangerous amount of momentum once it is cruising. 190 lbs is ridiculous.

In a recent development, but I also understand the appeal of this weird middle ground. The A9 Pro Max retains enough bicycle DNA that you can pedal it around and enjoy pedal assist, yet has enough battery and motor underneath you to deliver something much closer to small-motorcycle performance when you twist the throttle.

Imagine going off-road and getting to fly up hills while pedaling hard, but then being able to switch to throttle once your legs get worn out. Sure, it’s not everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s a cup of tea.

This bike is big. It’s heavy. It’s absurdly powerful by e-bike standards. And it absolutely isn’t the machine I’d recommend for someone looking for a normal street-legal electric bicycle.

But if what you actually want is a big, powerful electric two-wheeler that still lets you turn the pedals when the mood strikes, the Aniioki A9 Pro Max makes a surprisingly compelling argument for this increasingly bizarre category of pedal-equipped e-motos.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bitcoinmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

German Bundestag Lets Customs Freeze Crypto Over €100,000 Without a Criminal Case as the Bill Goes to the Bundesrat

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The German Bundestag on Thursday approved a government bill that would let customs freeze cryptocurrency and other assets worth more than €100,000 when their lawful origin appears implausible, without first opening a criminal case.
  • The Bundestag passed the Customs Financial Justice Act, a Finance Ministry overhaul to strengthen the customs administration and fight financial crime, on Nov.
  • Sources indicate that crypto is covered expressly, using the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets definition, but it is not singled out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The German Bundestag on Thursday approved a government bill that would let customs freeze cryptocurrency and other assets worth more than €100,000 when their lawful origin appears implausible, without first opening a criminal case. Permanent confiscation would still take a finance-court judgment. The measure still needs the Bundesrat’s consent before a planned Jan. 1, 2027 start, and the timing of that upper-house vote remains unclear.

The Bundestag passed the Customs Financial Justice Act, a Finance Ministry overhaul to strengthen the customs administration and fight financial crime, on Nov. 12. The federal government introduced the bill on Sept. 30. The Finance Committee recommended passage on Nov. 11, with the Christian Democrats, Social Democrats and Alternative for Germany in favor, The Left opposed and the Greens abstaining.

Sources indicate that crypto is covered expressly, using the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets definition, but it is not singled out. The same administrative procedure applies to cash, cars, real estate and other property. It reaches only “significant” assets: generally those worth more than €100,000, or more than €50,000 if the asset must be entered in a public register, such as vehicles or land. Because crypto is not registered that way, the €100,000 threshold applies. Customs may estimate the value, and closely related items can be treated as one asset.

Customs offices — not Germany’s Financial Intelligence Unit, which the same bill strengthens separately — may freeze those assets for up to 30 days without a criminal case if there are factual indications the origin is not lawful, meaning lawful acquisition “does not appear plausible.” A finance court may extend that hold once by 150 days. That extension is decided by a single judge, without a hearing, in an order that cannot be appealed. Filing a confiscation application stops the clock until the court rules, so the often-cited 180-day period is not a hard cap.

In a recent development, permanent confiscation still requires a finance-court panel to be convinced the origin is unlawful. The committee shifted that decision away from a single judge. Owners must be told they are not required to produce records, and anything they do provide may be used in tax and criminal cases. The official justification says mere silence, or a denial of knowledge, will as a rule not be enough to prevent confiscation.

Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said in August that if suspects cannot show assets were legally acquired, “the Porsche or the Rolex are gone for now.” In Thursday’s debate, Social Democrat Ingo Vogel told the Bundestag that criminally acquired assets do not enjoy constitutional property protection, and that the bill is “no automatic confiscation” and “no blanket reversal of the burden of proof.”.

The Bundesrat, in an earlier comment, had asked for a true burden-of-proof reversal and for the court extension to run up to 12 months, citing, among other things, “crypto concealment structures.” The government refused the fuller reversal and did not adopt the longer hold in the bill the Bundestag approved.

Germany’s Federal Bar Association opposes the bill, warning that vague terms and missing paperwork, including for inherited assets, should not be treated as proof of illegality. The German Bar Association also rejected the government draft. The Blockchain Bundesverband, commenting on the ministry draft, said the law needed to distinguish custodial, self-custodied and decentralized arrangements, because with a self-custodied wallet control “regularly lies with the holder of the private key,” and state access then exists only through measures against the person, not through third parties. The bill itself is silent on how, or whether, customs could take self-custodied keys. A freeze of crypto would be carried out by attachment under the Tax Code.

The government expects about €308 million a year in extra revenue from 2028 from the procedure as a whole, not from crypto alone. The Greens argued that figure is a sliver of Germany’s estimated €100 billion annual money-laundering volume.

In a recent development, the newly introduced power is separate from an earlier criminal case. In 2024, Saxony’s prosecutors, with the Federal Criminal Police Office, sold about 49,858 bitcoin from the Movie2k case between June 19 and July 12, for €2.64 billion. That sale was an emergency liquidation in a criminal proceeding, not an exercise of the administrative tool the Bundestag has now approved.
